Morrison & Forester Generally we agree with the staff recommendation We do have a problem with the grandfathering element. Currently Section 315.3 would not fix the inclusionary requirements to which a project is subject until the project has received a site or building permit. The staff report recognizes that fixing the inclusionary requirements at the date of issuing a building permit would be inequitable and instead has recommended the amendment to the inclusionary housing requirements would apply to projects until they receive Planning Commission approval. An amendment should apply to projects while they're pending the Planning Commission approval. However, even if staff's proposal is incorporated into section 315.3, it would still impose a great hardship on project sponsors by eliminating any certainty that these sponsors would have when they're negotiating their land purchases. The inclusionary housing requirements have a big impact on land value on how much a project sponsor can afford to pay for a piece of land. The number and subsidy level, below market-rate units that must be included is a key piece of information the sponsor needs before purchasing the land.  Without knowing what percentage must be constructed below market-rate will affect the subsidy of the units until after entitlement. Because Planning Commission approval for larger projects is not typically received until two years after a land purchase agreement has been executed.  Supervisor Maxwell's amendment even with staff's proposed change would require project sponsors to purchase land without having a solid idea of how much they can feasibly pay for that land. A more equitable solution would be to fix the provision of the inclusionary ordinance that would apply to a project sponsor on the date of filing of the project sponsor's first application for the project. The requirements would follow the project through its entitlement because the first application typically occurs after a land deal is finalized. Also, the Zoning Administrator and the Board of Supervisors agree there needs to be an exception within the inclusionary housing ordinance to deal with certain special care facilities such as residential care facilities for seniors with dementia. Two possible solutions is that the definition of rent should not include charges related to non-housing services including food services, medical care, personal assistance in these special care facilities. Another would be that the residential inclusionary housing affordable program should not regulate these special care facilities.

We'd like to suggest as Ms. Schindler has done that the grandfather clause be on the date of the first filing. And if in fact the Zoning Administrator makes a determination they are not, then there would be fair game for any changes in the BMR legislation. And just to ensure that there is transparency and an opportunity to appeal if there is a disagreement with the Zoning Administrator's yearly report that could be appealed to the Board of Appeals. Following are some suggestions the Zoning Administrator should take into account to ensure that people are not banking their application:  After there has been a planner assigned for the environment, that person should determine whether the project sponsor is taking advantage of having a scoping meeting, that following the scoping meeting the project sponsor has engaged a professional environmental consultant to press forward with the environmental evaluation.  He should also consider things like as or when the project sponsor has asked or responded to meetings to discuss design and other approvals; that prior to the time that either a negative declaration or EIR is published, that the project sponsor have filed all of the other needed applications and requests whether they be variances, whether they be conditional uses, whether they be 309 exceptions prior to the publication of the negative declaration and the EIR.

Pillsbury I'm a real estate and land use attorney at the Pillsbury firm here in San Francisco. I'd like to echo the remarks of the previous two speakers We have proposed an amendment that is very similar to the one that Morrison and Forester and Ms. Schindler's firm have proposed this week. We have added on language to address the concern about the rush to filing, and then the potential for the project sponsors to subsequently sit on the applications. What this carved out language basically does is looks back to the first application filing date. If you have an application on file prior to this ordinance becoming effective, then you are carved out. From there it goes on to basically say that you can't just sit on your application.  You have to continue to diligently pursue it with the Department. It is up to the Zoning Administrator to evaluate whether project sponsors are sitting on their applications. That is done through a series of criteria that the Zoning Administrator may look at to determine whether or not the project sponsor is still actively pursuing the application. That includes whether or not the sponsor has participated in a scoping meeting with MEA.  Subsequent to such a meeting, has the project sponsor engaged an environmental consultant to work with the department?  Then whether the project sponsor has filed all other applications with the department that would be necessary for a site or building permit to be issued for the project.  Then finally whether the project sponsor has hired an architect and submitted conceptual plans and has, subject to the department's resources, been able to meet with the department to go over the project design.  The Zoning Administrator would make that determination. If the project sponsor disagreed, the project sponsor would have the right to appeal that decision along the lines of any other type of Zoning Administrator appeals. We think this is a fair fix for the legislation. We think it's necessary, in any event, because the way the legislation is currently drafted, if you got your CU yesterday, it's unclear what your requirements are.

South of Market Community Action Network and South of Market (SOMA) Community We agree with the recommendations supervisor Maxwell has presented. On-site, off-site and in lieu. Council of Community Housing Organizations I'd like to substantially support staff's recommendation except in those areas that I disagree with staff's recommendation, which is twofold. We have proposed an amendment that we think will address one of Mr. Badiner's concerns, which is the definitional question of what is a project. There is a real world situation out there in which there's parcelization going on – sometimes three and four different parcels of two or three units have come in – although the total is nine or ten or 12 units, they come in under the 10. We have some language that we think will address that and also deal with Mr. Badiner's concern about defining what is a project in a little bit more rigorous way. First I'd like to speak to two other matters.  One is staff's recommendation that you not go forward on the off-site requirement, that you hold that for the study. I think that's a misplaced assumption that this is an economic issue. It's not an economic issue. It's basically a policy question. This City and County either supports inclusionary zoning on-site or it doesn't. The recommendation for a one-mile radius is I think a rational approach. 85, 90% of these projects are south of Market and east of Van Ness. 85, 90% of the potential off-site project sites are south of Market and east of Van Ness. No one has ever proposed doing a project in Rincon Hill and building the affordable housing in Pacific Heights. It's not going to happen. If you actually do the math, the one-mile radius I think is the reality of the situation. A majority of commissioners have repeatedly said we want the units on-site.  We don't want them off-site. That's what this legislation will guarantee. It's not an economic impact. The question is when should this apply? I'm happy to see that the big-time attorneys are arguing because at least some of them understand what the game is. That is parking and approval. Getting approval for a project at an old rate of fees and requirements and sitting on that project; and that you have no ability of hurrying that developer on. If we say they've got to pay the fees, in effect, when they pull their planning/building permit, which is what the ordinance does, they will pull their permit. We will ensure that these projects are built. They won't sit on it. I think the existing language is just fine. I would urge you to approve it.

Rubin and Junius Just a comment on the grandfather provision. Projects that have been approved and projects that are in the pipeline have already committed.  They're already invested. They have spent money; they have hired designers.  They are well down the road. The economics of the projects are fixed. To think about hitting those types of projects with new rules in simply unfair and it's something that has not been done in the past. Pipeline projects are traditionally grandfathered with these kinds of provisions and it is crucial that these rules not be changed so that they affect a large number of pipeline projects. The staff report lists I think 25 projects that have been approved and not yet pulled building permits. There are a whole bunch more that are stuck in the system and the system is slow. They're grinding it out doing the best they can. Those projects should not be penalized.

Deputy City Attorney Kate Stacy Wanted to talk a little about how the Commission adopts its minutes. Charter Section 4.104 requires all commissioners to vote yes or no on all matters unless that commissioner is excused by a vote of the Commission. Even where minutes are being adopted, commissioners may not be automatically excluded from that vote because they did not attend that meeting. The Commission could follow one of two routes: The Commissioners could vote on those minutes even though the commissioner was not present at that hearing because a vote on the minutes is different from a vote on a permit. It doesn't have the same adjudicative and due process implications. So a commissioner could vote on minutes for a meeting that you did not attend because you generally are aware of the accuracy of your secretary in transcribing the minutes. You may or may not get public comments on those minutes. You may or may not get commissioners comments on those minutes. Or you could review the file and the tape if you are interested in that meeting. But you can vote on the minutes without going back and reviewing the file and the tapes the way that commissioners are required to do on a permit. The other option for the Commission is to actually vote to excuse a commissioner from voting on the minutes. That would have to be a separate action taken by the Commission each time the vote is made. I just wanted to make sure the Commission was aware of that requirement and to think about how you want to vote on the minutes. Even if you weren't present at a meeting, I wanted to be sure that the individual commissioners were aware that you could vote on those minutes based on other evidence in the record.

Morrison & Forester Generally we agree with the staff recommendation We do have a problem with the grandfathering element. Currently Section 315.3 would not fix the inclusionary requirements to which a project is subject until the project has received a site or building permit. The staff report recognizes that fixing the inclusionary requirements at the date of issuing a building permit would be inequitable and instead has recommended the amendment to the inclusionary housing requirements would apply to projects until they receive Planning Commission approval. An amendment should apply to projects while they're pending the Planning Commission approval. However, even if staff's proposal is incorporated into section 315.3, it would still impose a great hardship on project sponsors by eliminating any certainty that these sponsors would have when they're negotiating their land purchases. The inclusionary housing requirements have a big impact on land value on how much a project sponsor can afford to pay for a piece of land. The number and subsidy level, below market-rate units that must be included is a key piece of information the sponsor needs before purchasing the land.  Without knowing what percentage must be constructed below market-rate will affect the subsidy of the units until after entitlement. Because Planning Commission approval for larger projects is not typically received until two years after a land purchase agreement has been executed.  Supervisor Maxwell's amendment even with staff's proposed change would require project sponsors to purchase land without having a solid idea of how much they can feasibly pay for that land. A more equitable solution would be to fix the provision of the inclusionary ordinance that would apply to a project sponsor on the date of filing of the project sponsor's first application for the project. The requirements would follow the project through its entitlement because the first application typically occurs after a land deal is finalized. Also, the Zoning Administrator and the Board of Supervisors agree there needs to be an exception within the inclusionary housing ordinance to deal with certain special care facilities such as residential care facilities for seniors with dementia. Two possible solutions is that the definition of rent should not include charges related to non-housing services including food services, medical care, personal assistance in these special care facilities. Another would be that the residential inclusionary housing affordable program should not regulate these special care facilities.

McCarthy and Schwartz Ditto to the comments of Ms. Schindler. I too agree that the administrative issues are best served by having staff and the Mayor's office of Housing work those out. Following are some suggestions the Zoning Administrator should take into account to ensure that people are not banking their application:  After there has been a planner assigned for the environment, that person should determine whether the project sponsor is taking advantage of having a scoping meeting, that following the scoping meeting the project sponsor has engaged a professional environmental consultant to press forward with the environmental evaluation.  He should also consider things like as or when the project sponsor has asked or responded to meetings to discuss design and other approvals; that prior to the time that either a negative declaration or EIR is published, that the project sponsor have filed all of the other needed applications and requests whether they be variances, whether they be conditional uses, whether they be 309 exceptions prior to the publication of the negative declaration and the EIR.

Pillsbury I'm a real estate and land use attorney at the Pillsbury firm here in San Francisco. I'd like to echo the remarks of the previous two speakers We have proposed an amendment that is very similar to the one that Morrison and Forester and Ms. Schindler's firm have proposed this week. We have added on language to address the concern about the rush to filing, and then the potential for the project sponsors to subsequently sit on the applications. What this carved out language basically does is looks back to the first application filing date. If you have an application on file prior to this ordinance becoming effective, then you are carved out. From there it goes on to basically say that you can't just sit on your application.  You have to continue to diligently pursue it with the Department. It is up to the Zoning Administrator to evaluate whether project sponsors are sitting on their applications. That is done through a series of criteria that the Zoning Administrator may look at to determine whether or not the project sponsor is still actively pursuing the application. That includes whether or not the sponsor has participated in a scoping meeting with MEA.  Subsequent to such a meeting, has the project sponsor engaged an environmental consultant to work with the department?  Then whether the project sponsor has filed all other applications with the department that would be necessary for a site or building permit to be issued for the project.  Then finally whether the project sponsor has hired an architect and submitted conceptual plans and has, subject to the department's resources, been able to meet with the department to go over the project design.  The Zoning Administrator would make that determination. If the project sponsor disagreed, the project sponsor would have the right to appeal that decision along the lines of any other type of Zoning Administrator appeals. We think this is a fair fix for the legislation. We think it's necessary, in any event, because the way the legislation is currently drafted, if you got your CU yesterday, it's unclear what your requirements are.

Deputy City Attorney Kate Stacy Wanted to talk a little about how the Commission adopts its minutes. Charter Section 4.104 requires all commissioners to vote yes or no on all matters unless that commissioner is excused by a vote of the Commission. Even where minutes are being adopted, commissioners may not be automatically excluded from that vote because they did not attend that meeting. The Commission could follow one of two routes: The Commissioners could vote on those minutes even though the commissioner was not present at that hearing because a vote on the minutes is different from a vote on a permit. It doesn't have the same adjudicative and due process implications. So a commissioner could vote on minutes for a meeting that you did not attend because you generally are aware of the accuracy of your secretary in transcribing the minutes. You may or may not get public comments on those minutes. You may or may not get commissioners comments on those minutes. Or you could review the file and the tape if you are interested in that meeting. But you can vote on the minutes without going back and reviewing the file and the tapes the way that commissioners are required to do on a permit. The other option for the Commission is to actually vote to excuse a commissioner from voting on the minutes. That would have to be a separate action taken by the Commission each time the vote is made. I just wanted to make sure the Commission was aware of that requirement and to think about how you want to vote on the minutes. Even if you weren't present at a meeting, I wanted to be sure that the individual commissioners were aware that you could vote on those minutes based on other evidence in the record.

Zipcar There is a section of the language in C-3 that attempts to revise the definition of car sharing that is recommended by the transportation research board that concerns us to a degree. We understand the car sharing definition is necessary for the C-3 legislation and just submit that the language in the draft be modified to reflect the generally accepted definition of car sharing nationwide. We feel that the current transportation research board recommended definition sufficient to identify true car sharing operations:  with  the membership program alternative to car ownership program such that persons or entities permitted to use vehicles from a fleet on an hourly basis. We feel that certification process would increase costs for car sharing operators in the city while creating a level of geography that would stifle the growth and important transportation solution for San Francisco residents. Other cities have policies that are successfully stimulating growth in this category and without a burdensome certification process or more elaborate definition. Basically what we're saying is there is already a definition generally accepted around the country and in this legislation it seems that you Re just trying to create another level of definition and trying to be creative. We recommend that developers be allowed to choose a car-sharing operator based on competitive assessment. We are in strong support of C-3. We think it is a great benefit to the city, for residents and something we would certainly like to participate in. We're worried about the burdensome effect and the costs associated with the certification process and the level of bureaucracy this may create.

Executive Director of Transportation for a Livable City I have to honest, I don't love this legislation that much any more. It is definitely the product of compromise. But is has been through the process. At least we have a broad consensus.  This is all something we can all live with. It is a big step forward for this city. One of the things that concern me is the provision about how building facades can be treated. The other thing I think is important is car sharing.  We have a certification project process at BART that is very similar after the process that is in here that does not prove burdensome. We think it is important actually to make sure what is being called car sharing is really doing what we want it to do, which is increase the amount of walking and cycling, increase transit use, and decrease dependence on automobiles. I don't think that provision should prove burdensome because it is not for us. Lastly, I would say that there are two unchaptered provisions. One thing we found in our previous discussion is we do have studies that show lower parking ratios decreased traffic. The idea that we could do a more comprehensive study, generate a little more light and heat around this question of parking affects travel behaviors – what does unbundling do, what does car sharing do, how do people downtown really get around?  Are they driving to work, walking, et cetera? That is in here. I'm really hoping that is the study that gets funded and done this year. We are going to add even with this legislation, 8,000 new parking spaces for the downtown's unanticipated units. If we get it wrong we're going to screw up downtown. The City's streetscape master plan that was adopted by the Commission in 1996 does a lot to enhance the streetscape, but I think we need to revise streetscape planning in the Planning Department. I'm hoping that the follow up to this study will also appear in your current budget. Sue Hester We can't seem to do legislation without a major soap opera in this city. One of the more controversial proposals the last time around was the requirement that parking be pushed out. That was one of the things that set off developers. The compromise that is in here is about the three stories above grade is still going to be a problem. The above ground garages in the downtown generally are bad citizens, and three stories above ground is a lot.  They are noise, they are pollution, and they are generally ugly. One compromise that has good intentions is that you get to have one to one parking if it is a two-bedroom unit. I think it was the presentation you hade recently on the economic report where a shocking proportion of San Francisco is self-employed people.  There are a lot of people that have no offices that have more than a one-bedroom unit and work at home. The Planning Department doesn't monitor whether two-bedroom and three-bedroom units actually are family housing. We need to do a reality check on that.  You need to commit yourself to figuring out who occupies two-bedroom units and go back and revise this. If all you are doing is saying you are self-employed and you should use your second bedroom as an office, it's a one to one parking requirement. I think that's the way it is. Robert McCarthy of McCarthy and Schwartz I stand to commend the staff. We would urge you to adopt the recommendation of the staff, including the modification proposed by the staff. I think Ms. Hester is right about the past.  Many people have in fact abused their entitlements. We would urge you to adopt the legislation as proposed by staff.

for the Project Sponsor I think all of you are aware of the site, 1844 Market It is adjacent to the LGBT Center, Lincoln parting lot, and the old Sue Mills site. Representing the Homeowners Association The initial study says that the project is consistent with the proposed Octavia Plan. That is not really relevant now. However, even under that plan, the height proposed here would exceed the maximum in that Plan of 85 feet on Market Street because the project proponents want to measure the 85 feet from the height or the high side of the property – the corner right next to our building. As it slopes down towards Market Street, the result would be that it would actually be higher than the 85 feet allowed on Market Street under the proposed Plan. Why can't the design be compatible on the Waller Street side with the residential character–lower character–and if it is desirable to have a complete coverage on the Market Street side, that can be accomplished as well. The evidence set forth in the report is inconsistent with the conclusion that this eight-story building, plus mechanical over the top of that is inconsistent with the vicinity. Thus the findings actually admit it is incompatible with the character of that part of the neighborhood. I want to note that there is a depiction in the materials that is misleading because it makes it look as though an 80-foot building is slightly taller than our building, which is four stories and 40 feet tall. There is a traffic problem in the neighborhood. There is never any parking on the street. It is very important that the residents who move in there have a place to park their cars. The loading zone is important here from experience. I know there is no place for anyone, even if they have a loading zone. It will be very dangerous.  You can't see around cars and it is already crowded out there. The traffic flow will be impacted by this many people coming and going. There is no stop sign there and it is full of traffic because everyone uses the streets parallel to Waller now to get onto the freeway entrance. William I think it is a gross misrepresentation to suggest that this project will be occupied by less than an automobile population that is less than downtown. It will be a selling point for the project that you can get from this project onto the freeway more easily than in any other point in San Francisco. There is no retail loading on Market Street. All of the retail loading is designed to take place on Waller Street All of the garbage collection is going to take place on Waller Street. There is no provision for move-in or move-out, which is required for any project. Right now there is a school across the street.  In the morning parents bring their kids there and drop them off. Waller Street becomes impassable between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. in the morning. To this existing situation on Waller Street, you are now going to add garbage, loading for the retail, and the 85 cars coming out of the building to go to work. The problem is a ten-pound project in a five-pound bag. The project treats Waller Street as an access alley. I think this is a wonderful site. I think there needs to be more design work and I would recommend that you require that design work before you grant entitlement to the project. Gilbert Criswell I sympathize with my neighbors to the north of Market But this development will bring a new day for my neighborhood and community as well as San Francisco. It will bring new life to an area that has been neglected for decades. I have lived across from the address of 1844 Market Street for more than 12 years. 12 years of blight, litter, dirt and prostitution, used needles, broken condoms and alcoholics. More over, it has been 12 years of living with limited choice in retail. Sound government policy and process should be part of your decision-making process by this commission. I urge the Commission to take the advice of its own department staff and approve it. Listen to the voice of reason from a person that will be directly impacted by this development. Rebecca Rice I have lived across the street from the proposed project at 19 Pearl Street for over 15 years. I'm very much in favor of the project. I think this would make Market Street starting at Octavia Boulevard the visual gateway to upper Market. I also think this will spur further improvement in the blocks around both the Castro and Van Ness. The design of the building I think is right for the location.  It looks very nice. As far as the transit is concerned, I commute on the S Market to downtown in the morning between 7 and 8 a.m.  It runs every ten minutes and hardly has any people on it.  There are dozens of bus lines going in all different directions.  I don't think that would be an impact. Dale Risden I own the property at 1870 Market Street. I'm immediately adjacent.  The Gay Community Center is on one side of the project; I'm located on the other. I participated in the Market Octavia Plan.  I've also participated in improvements in that area. This is a derelict lot.  It has been derelict for years. I literally recently had to move my business off of Market Street because I couldn't continue to have my employees harassed. I am so happy to see this development. Over the last year and a half, this development has made every opportunity to meet with me, ask what concerns I had, what improvements ought to be made. I saw them meet with the Hayes Valley Association who actually created the Market Octavia Plan.  They're the ones that have let the effort. It is really hard for me to understand at this late moment why they are making objections when all along they've had opportunity to be able to do things to change the building in a better way. I'd also like to state that following the Market Octavia Plan, when I develop my property, I'm looking at a 7-story building and intend to provide absolutely no parking because I can't do it coming off of Market. Any future development there, according to the Market Plan, will have no parking unless you have access to the rear of another street. That's what future development will be. The block is derelict and this will completely change that neighborhood. I look forward to its construction. Peter Howells I'm a resident and homeowner at Octavia and Hayes Street, about two blocks away from the project. I'm also a small business owner who owns the café directly adjacent to the property. I've been walking past that property for many years as a resident. As has been stated before, this is one of the biggest eyesores on Market Street between Van Ness and Castro.  It is a magnet for garbage, graffiti, homeless, even when partially occupied by the previous owner, Sue Mills, it would often become an encampment. A large abandoned property continues to attract garbage and is unattractive for street traffic, which is not good for my business. I'm in strong support of development in general on that property and I feel they have done much to get comment and feedback from the neighborhood. As a business owner and resident, I feel satisfied that Bay Rock has addressed the concerns I had in the community meetings while remaining a viable sort of residential and commercial development. They have produced a design that will benefit both our block as a business, but also the neighborhood in general. It is attractive and is consistent with recent residential development in the City that has also drawn public praise. Adam Millard-Ball I live about two blocks from the proposed development. I am also a Board member of the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association. We would like to acknowledge the efforts the staff and developers have made. This design is vastly improved from what we saw last year. We really are looking for something that sets the tome here for future development on this stretch of Market Street and is also consistent with the Market Octavia Plan. Our only concern is Waller Street. We hope planning staff can address those for the developers as they go forward. The main issue relates to parking. This development is proposing .75 spaces per unit, which is actually quite a bit more than the maximum that would be allowed by right in the Market Octavia Plan. .75 spaces are allowed only by conditional use, such as unbundling of parking. We are also cognizant of the need to secure parking in this development. The neighborhood supports less parking for several reasons:  This is a half block from the new freeway off ramp and we don't want this to be a kind of bedroom development for Silicon Valley where people just can park and then drive onto the freeway in the morning. We hope to ensure that people live and shop in the neighborhood. It is also an issue of attracting lower income households as well. Overall we really appreciate the fact that the developers have come a long way.  It is a much better development than it was. Raising the benchmark should be the Market Octavia Plan. We really hope that when this comes before you, you take prompt action to approve a Plan according to its original spirit because without it, it makes it very difficult for the Neighborhood Association. We're looking at each project on a very piecemeal basis, which is not the best use of anyone's time and also brings less consistency between developments.

Castro Area Planning and Action We support bike, transit oriented infill projects on Market Street and other goals of the Market Octavia Plan such as reduced parking and traffic calming. More active uses on Market Street help to create pedestrian friendly environment that strengthens the ties between the Castro Area and Octavia Street, especially the Gay and Lesbian Community Center. Parking should not be a requirement in this area at all. While we are glad to finally see projects with less than one to one parking in this area, we would support even less parking. While the massing of the project is varies and responsive to the scale of the other buildings on the Market Street side, the architectural expression and detailing leave much to be desired. The Waller Street side of the project needs to be more responsive to the residential scale of the street, especially at the sidewalk level. This project will set the standard for future development in the corridor, and as a PUD, high quality design is required. Robin Levitt I'm on the Board of the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association. I live at Lilly Street and Octavia, which is abut two and a half blocks from this project. Contrary to what you've heard earlier today about Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association opposing this project, and why I'm not speaking for the neighborhood Association, I think in general the neighborhood looks very favorably upon this project. It is true that the block is very blighted and this project will do a lot to enhance the neighborhood. It will also add much needed housing to the neighborhood. So we generally support this project. And I appreciate all the work that Bay Rock and the architects have done to work with the community to develop a building that enhances this part of the neighborhood. They have really come a long way in developing the design for this project. Having said that, I just have a couple of concerns about the project. I want to echo what was previously said about parking. The Market Octavia Plan does call for .5 spaces per unit and I think that this project should be consistent with the Market Octavia Plan. The Market Street bike route and the Valencia Street bike route converge there. I think it is very important that this project provide secure accessible bike parking, at least one bike space per unit. Another point I'd like to make is about the architecture. As I said, the design of the project has evolved and it's gotten much better. This is a prominent site. It is actually two buildings–one building facing Market Street, and one building facing Waller Street. The Waller Street side really deserves to address some of the residential character of that side of the project. The Market Street side is very prominent.  It is a gateway to the city.  It is a gateway to the Castro.  It is also a gateway from the freeway.  So it really deserves extra attention. I hope the Planning Department will continue to work with them on that. David Dupree I'm a member of the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association but I'm speaking for myself only. I've been at meeting between the Association and the developers where they have listened to us and taken into account our comments and seemed to be very responsive.  I commend them for that. One of the projects of our Association has become a thing called  living Streets. I have talked to a Project Manager at Bay Rock and he's been receptive to coordinating with the potential developer of the next block to create a living street. One thing I've worked on is putting art on the walls of the buildings.  He has been willing to look at being involved–bringing art or sculpture to Waller Street. I believe this would affect any blandness of architecture along there. I do support the .75 parking. I've talked with a number of residents in the area and they are indicating their willingness to even pay for parking spaces, for a dedicated parking space off-street of $150 to $200 a month.  Because most of the parking in the area is on street or in rather inaccessible garages. I walk through the area every morning at 8:15 a.m. More mornings than not, the traffic does move along Haight, along Oak and into the area so that I've actually timed particular cars not taking more than five minutes to actually get onto the freeway.

Transportation for a Livable City Many speakers said this is a prime location for housing that is oriented to transit, walking and bicycling.  There are a number of things that we'd love to see in this project. One would be car sharing.  There is no car share pod that is immediately adjacent, but putting a City Car Share pos in this project would be great. The other is unbundling parking. That is a requirement in the Rincon Hill Plan that would be required in C-3 later today. It is just a good idea to do. The third thing I'd say is the importance of secure bike parking. In the Rincon Hill Plan and in the C-3 legislation there is a requirement for secure bike parking; I believe it is one space for every other unit.  There is also a requirement that bike parking be secure–a bike room or bike lockers.  And not down in the garage.  You should be able to access the bike parking without having to go up and down the ramp the cars use because that is dangerous. As was mentioned, this is at the intersection of the two most important bike routes of the city–Market Street and Valencia Street.  It is a great location for cycling. I'd ask you to have secure parking as a condition of approval as well as accessibility, not using the ramps that the cars use.

Head of Bay Rock Residential When we first discovered the site, I was asked for help by being told that there was this great expanse of eyesore. We set up coordination with Neighborhood Services to police the site and secure the site. I was asked to create some active retail here. The long frontage we're creating, wide expanses of glass replace dead space and gathering spots for all the images and figures that have been out there. We have about 5500 feet that increases the livability of the neighborhood.  It also acts as a welcoming entry statement to the community itself. More importantly, the proposal for retail here leverages the great asset of Market Street. Our strategy with this is not to get rich off the retail.  We are creating a lot of value upstairs in the development. But we made a commitment to the neighborhood not to use formula retail. We want to be actively outreaching.  We've done significant outreach with about 26 Market Street businesses similar to the Buy Rite People.  We'd love to have those people in there. The market community, grocer community is telling us they can't compete with Safeway that close. However, we feel we can still gain some sort of type of hybrid in the area. So we're very hopeful and positive about activating the street but we're not going to get rich on it. We're going to subsidize it because we think it sets the tone for the eye level portion of this. On the residential design on Waller Street, we've made significant eye level improvements there as well. It is occupied by stoops along Waller as well as garage doors. We've given several schemes to staff. We're working on the details. I think it is going to be very neighborhood contextually friendly on that side of the street and I appreciate your support here today.

Project Sponsor I'm one of the owners of what is going to be the Buy Rite Creamery ice cream shop located across the street from the market I've owned the last 8 years–Buy Rite Market. It's going to be independently owned by myself and my wife and Chris. Buy Rite Market has been in my family since 1964. Our family has had a presence and been involved in the community for the past 42 years. We have been great supporters of our local community. We hire as much as we possibly can from the local neighbors. We work really hard with the businesses in the community to support each other and to provide the services that the neighborhood needs. We feel that the ice cream shop is small and will be a nice addition to the neighborhood. It will provide a great amenity for visitors to Delores Park. The ice cream itself is going to be made in-house. We're going to be using dairy from a family owned local organic farm based in Marin. We're going to use all organic fruits for our sorbets and making our own cookies and cakes for the ice cream cakes we'll be making as well. The ice cream will be made in small batches. It's all about being fresh and spontaneous with the seasons.

comment: My question is, who got this policy in advance of the hearing? I know I did because I asked for it. The problem we have with policies that have multiple hearings is people lose track of them. The people that are concerned about dwelling init mergers are neighborhood people and organizations and people who deal with affordable housing. I don't know anyone who got this. I want to know who got this. What input has there been since the last hearing? Are people aware of it?

There is a case that will be coming in front of you concerning the cinema 21 building and the building that was built wit it at the time. There is a roof with matching tiles on the building adjacent to it and on the other side there was a building with matching tiles. Apple Computer wants to take a fifth of the tiles and leave the other four fifths there. I want you to consider character. A major corporation comes in and wants to change something that has been since 1927. I want you to look at this issue. I will try to get you pictures.
