section: ITEM 17 WAS TAKEN OUT OF ORDER AND HEARD AFTER ITEM 11
comment: Co-Project Sponsor We held open houses for our neighbors to talk with us about the project. As far as we know all our neighbors approve of this. Tenant (did not state name) I wanted to vote my support for their application and confirm that it was clear from the beginning that I would be staying for a short time. I have another place I'm moving into.

I'm a long time resident in the Haight. I live across 529 Clayton and one block away from 409 Clayton. I am aware of how the free clinic worked in the past. I got a copy of the Master Plan. Some of my concerns are that they have expansion plans with some of the programs at 558. I am concerned about what is going to happen with the buildings they are vacating. You have mentioned Prop I. The Health Department has not informed neighbors in my neighborhood when they put a new program in. Prop I indicates if you pit in a new program you have to notify the neighbors. We are not notified. I'm concerned because the report indicated that the Haight/Ashbury Youth outreach program has been closed since 2005. They are in operation in my neighborhood. We have made the Planning Department aware of misuses of conditional use permits in my neighborhood and they have not done anything about it. If there is a conditional use, I'm interested in who's taking over and what is the status of the building and an answer to why the conditional use permits were not enforced. Marian We have a lot of problems with the free clinics. It's important for us to know what's happening in the neighborhood and what they plan to do. I feel we need to be informed. Not 30 days before it will go into place. I think it is important that they follow the same guidelines that everyone else has to. Ted Lowenberg The point that Mr. Badiner made is correct. The purpose of the Institutional Master Plan is to make the public aware of what is on the mind of the Haight-Ashbury Free Clinic, and response or prepare or do what you might do with that. My point is I think it's important in order for the public to know what's in the Master Plan and for them to give you, as planning commissioners the opportunity to comment and give input. A public hearing is warranted. Otherwise it goes into the pile of papers that exist in planning and it never sees the light of day in the neighborhood. I also got a copy of this document after I requested it 5 years ago. I think there are a lot of things in here that give me concerns – like telling the youth how to inject their drugs properly. To me that is a disconnect in healthy lifestyles and life skills building programs. I suppose there are other landmines like this in this document. The public review would bring this to light and give everybody an opportunity to scrutinize this for this type of disconnect and analyze what they will get. The area around Mission and Division is a neighborhood in Valencia that is struggling for its existence.

name_raw: Jim Meko, Chair of the Western SOMA Citizen's Task Force
role_title: Chair of the Western SOMA Citizen's Task Force
comment: This past Sunday we had a booth at the Folsom Street Fair. We were located between a porn studio and a sexual lubricant. It's amazing how many people wanted to talk about planning. Last night we had a meeting of the full task force. Western Soma Task Force has been in existence for a year. We have so many balls in the air; so many initiatives going in different directions that we organize an agenda and everybody came to report on what they are doing. The planning framework, the principles you have seen developed. The work on the residential enclave district, job retention, and creation. We are off to parks and open space and recreation; the issues of affordability. It was such an exciting meeting and at the end we gave ourselves an ovation. Insights came out of this. One is the need for boom proof zoning. Zoning that when you are doing cutting edge type zoning and you don't know the possible ramifications there would be a trigger mechanism or circuit breaker set in. If you detect a spike in some new use you have allowed that perhaps could get out of control [like live/work], then business services that would kick in and would go to effect so we wouldn't spend a year and a half yelling at you to do something about it. Another is in the south of market when you are dealing with large parcels of land like the Tennis Club, you can't devote them to housing. If we are talking about mixed use you need to find a split – 50% housing. If you devote the entire parcel to housing the goal of mixed use is a failure. Jim Salinas, Sr. Representing Carpenters Local 22 We come before you with a lot of land use issues because there are labor issues that effect San Francisco's working men and women that make up the work force in San Francisco. We come here weekly because we support projects where we have good citizens who decided to select fair contractors, meaning those individuals that are willing to pay the men and women a fair wage. When the project sponsors are here and bring labor they are saying we bring great public benefit. We are a great resource that drives the local economics in the city. What we make here we spend here. When we come to you and support good contractors, it means the resources of this city are not being taxed. When non-union contractors come before you they bring people from outside the city. I have gone into the field and found people at $10 an hour and no benefits. If they get hurt they go to General Hospital. If they or their families get sick they go to General Hospital. Please understand that the issues that we bring to you may not be land use specific issues but they are issues that you have direct decision-making ability over and the ability to benefit San Francisco as a whole. This past Sunday we had a booth at the Folsom Street Fair. We were located between a porn studio and a sexual lubricant. It's amazing how many people wanted to talk about planning. Last night we had a meeting of the full task force. Western Soma Task Force has been in existence for a year. We have so many balls in the air; so many initiatives going in different directions that we organize an agenda and everybody came to report on what they are doing. Judy Berkowitz I would like to speak on the community improvements of the Eastern Neighborhoods. You heard an informational report last week. Prior to Public Comment, you heard from other people and you favorably indicated you would look on bringing this back to the Commission. However, you stopped short of making a motion. I would like to request you to move to bring this back as an action item. I think that your authority as the Planning Commission is all parts of planning within the city and this needs to be heard by you and you need to give direction to the Board of Supervisors on what you think about this. I am not entirely sure, but I believe you were quoted as saying that you supported the item wholeheartedly in yesterday's Land Use Committee hearing and I do not think you gave that direction. I could be mistaken. Marilyn In several instances the question of legislation – whether appropriately it came before you or not – that issue has been raised. I would like to bring to your attention an ordinance reported to you last week that was introduced and that is a CEQA ordinance, which is an amendment of the Administrative Code, Chapter 31, which are our local CEQA controls. You were told it didn't need to come before you because it is not a Planning Code amendment. However, if you look at that Chapter 31 and section 3104, which sets responsibility. You need to schedule public hearing and the public needs to have the opportunity to speak to you on this. The Board of Supervisors for one reason or another is writing legislation they are putting on the fast track and are sending it through. You are getting short changed and the public is as well. It is not good public process and does not make the public happy. Sue Hestor I want to talk about the lack of implementation of a landmark historic designation. The city adopted the Dog Patch District in 2003. In 2005 a permit was approved without referral to Landmarks and it was a demolition. There were two hearings at the DBI and Board of Appeals as well as a forced action under the Permit Streamlining Act filing on the city on the 30 th or 29 th of August. After the forced action I didn't see a report to you. Implementation means that the Planning staff has to be notified when plans are adopted. That means at a very bear minimum, all of the people in the quadrant should have been notified. The cases on Tennessee Street, the permits were applied for in 1999, which is another serious issue. I don't understand why they hang around for six years. But since we are dealing with a whole lot of rezoning of a lot of historic districts that are about to be created in the Eastern Neighborhoods, if staff doesn't figure out now how to implement at the staff level so it never happens again. I am asking you to start thinking about implementation of your plans because project review and long-term planning don't meet. And permit review is where the projects are approved.

name_raw: Toni, representing Cohn and Mike Quinn-Lynn
comment: There has been much community involvement and input and cooperation with others on the development of the plan. Our proposal should be consistent with the Leeland Avenue streetscape plan and provide a street front. This street front on the garage would promote economic viability for small businesses and enhance Leeland Avenue. The project is well served by MUNI and Cal Train. In order to rehabilitate the structure we think this variance application is reasonable and a logical request. With direction from Mr. Nikitas, we have gone through many designs. We are proposing a second tree where the curb cut would be. We thought the project was well received by the Alliance and we believe we have made the required findings. We request that you approve our project as proposed. Sue Hestor When you pull up this site in the Assessor's records on the computer at Planning, you find the initial proposal was to do this along with 199 Leland. It is currently listed on Greg's list for sale vacant retail next door. They built that building. It went from three units to six by claiming it was senior housing. As a result of that there is an open space on that site compared to the regular planning code. The rents that are been offered are still really high for senior housing. This is the third senior housing project that is a problem. They can't sell at market rate to seniors because they don't have that income. The honest way to understand the project is to know this project is next to a vacant storefront. It appeared to be unoccupied senior housing units with unresolved issues about whether the city will allow a condo map for the six unit senior housing project next door. That is my observation. Mike Quinlin, property owner We thought we were buying one property – one fence around it. In escrow it showed as two properties. We, in accordance with the planning code, built a senior housing complex. It allows us double density. There were six apartments. We got the certificate last December. We have not rented all six. We are trying to get the building to carry itself. There is not a conspiracy housing that we can't find seniors to live there. We are unsuccessful in renting out the space. Leland Avenue is going to be a fine street eventually. When the library goes in across the road and when people develop, we will have a commercial strip that will be nice. We are ahead and we have been unable to get a commercial tenant in there. When we applied for the building we were going to build a condominium. You must apply at the time you build it. If we get the condo – we haven't. If we get it in three years time and a senior wants a condo, I want to sell it to them. I want the option to do that.

son of DR requestor This particular lot is substandard in relation to the neighborhood It is the smallest lot in the area. We oppose because the owner is proposing to build a third story on the smallest lot in the neighborhood. There are no other third story houses on all sides of the block.  In addition, we able to see portions of the Bay Bridge and slight portions of downtown from the backyard. The addition will have a flat roof and will not provide for that and will obstruct that. The addition is basically above our existing roofline. The windows look in our front yard.  It's in the kitchen. There are no exits from the back of the house.  If there is a fire in the kitchen, which is a typical fire prone area for a house, there are no exits provided. A flat roof would have drains built inside of the roof.  This person put the drains on the outside. One of the other problems with the development is the backyard is eight feet in width on a downward, hilly location. The owner developed a backyard with patios. This house sits down into a cave like.  It doesn't provide much sun.  This worsens the situation. This area is near Candlestick.  We have to move our cars off the street during game events. This proposal is changing the character of the area. All of the houses in the area are afforded with a decent backyard. This person took it upon themselves to develop this extended property.  It has been done. During construction, the sidewalk on our side of the house was broken up. Brian, property owner He said a few things that I don't think were exactly accurate. There are no windows facing the back of this house. This house extended all the way to the property line. There are not windows facing from his side of the house to the property that I am working on. In addition, the property was not extended additionally to the backyard. We are requesting to change the roof from pitch to flat but it's not actually flat.  It actually slopes slightly and that's why the gutters are on the back.  That's an issue he brought up. When they requested a DR, the said they were concerned because there would be personal entertaining in the front of the property. I plan to move there.  I hope to move there. I currently live down the street in a one-bedroom house and no garage or parking with two children and a wife. We want this house.  It has a garage. I never entertained in front of my house and have no intentions of entertaining in the front of this one. The other issues about it blocking the sun are not issues and are not accurate. It is not a three-story building. Mary Bryant, DR requestor (spoke during rebuttal) We were not informed of the first variance request to oppose that request. We discussed it with staff and we were told there was a mark on the drawing where a door was removed and a bathroom was there. Staff told us the bathroom was going to be removed. This project has moved it.  Originally it was said it was going to be a workshop on the first floor then a work out room.  Now it's a home office. We know this person is an investor and realtor. We believe he is developing it. Again, the community utilizes their backyards.  There are kids out here and when game days happen they take advantage of their backyards and play in their backyards.  Just because this house was carved on a small lot this person shouldn't be afforded to extend the house. [I'm sorry] we missed the opportunity to comment on the variance to extend the backyard.

We are here to seek authorization for this project. The project will benefit the neighborhood and the other retail uses near by. It's a small bank, 2 enclosed ATM's in a 118 square feet vestibule. This is important to First Republic and its customers. It operates a branch in the neighborhood on Stockton and Jackson. The banks newest ATM is in the Embarcadero Center. We believe the project will be good for the neighborhood because it will increase pedestrian traffic on the east side of Columbus. The owners of the building have had a lot of difficulty retaining quality retail tenants because of the foot traffic. The intersection is not a conducive location to foot traffic. The location is unobtrusive. The entrance is recessed under the upper stories. As we discussed in the September 26 letter, it meets design criteria for space ATM's, lock doors, appropriate lighting and cameras. We request that you approve this project. Scott Robertson, Building Owner I've owned this building for 13 years. This building needs your help. You are in the position to help this building and the community. This building is an island. No one walks by. It needs a lot of help. I reduced their rent $500 so they could afford to stay. Retail all around me is failing.

Policy Director of the Planning and Research Commission (SPUR) I really support the plan of action that has been laid out by staff. I think it is sensible. I enjoyed hearing your discussion about the organization by topic so you see the plan an an integrated whole. I appreciate the suggestion there should be a time certain. I know there are a lot of people who want to attend the hearings and it is a helpful way to move forward. SPUR has been supportive of the Better Neighborhood's planning process. The reason we are supportive is because it provides certainty to the community. It provides certainty to project sponsors and they know what to build. I believe the process is laid before you and it will allow us the time to participate in the discussion. I hope you move the initiation forward.

President of the Duboce Triangle Neighborhood Association We are 20% of the plan area. We are cited as a model neighborhood in a transit rich environment. We support long range planning. We support a plan sensitive to the needs of our neighborhood. I want to acknowledge the work the Planning Department has done.  They have been accessible to us. We have spent a hundred hours on this plan. We have some concerns remaining.  Some are serious. The historical survey. We feel we are inches apart. We are looking at a 30-year plan. I don't understand why three more months will kill this thing. When you rezone you give a benefit to the property owner. If it comes back different you will take away the benefits from the property owner and there will be a reason for the property owner being in a historic district. We feel zoning is good for preservation. We want to do a full court press and understand where the properties are that are historic and where the individual sites are. When do the infrastructure improvements kick in? We welcome the way the process is going in terms of set dates. Separate parking and historic preservation. There will be workshops with the neighborhood groups to vet out the issues. We support that if there is a real chance to make changes.

Served on the Task Force of the [Duboce] Triangle Area. We have been working with staff for about a year. Our initial comments cane in August.  We have read the plan and all the material. We have offered thoughtful suggestions on how this plan should be amended so that can we can embrace it. Right now we are not ready to embrace this plan. We are here to appeal to you, the Commissioner, as you go through this, to listen to our rational. To hear why we think in our neighborhood certain aspects of this plan will be detrimental rather than beneficial. We researched and read it an thoughtfully considered the issues. We had heated discussions in our group on whether the plan is good for us or not. We need these amendments and I hope over the next few months that the staff and the Commisison will be open to the changes we are putting forth, which we think will improve the plan and protect our neighborhood. As you review this information, please keep in mind that there are rebuilding and reweaving neighborhoods that are putting things back together. The Triangle is not that the type of neighborhood.  It's already a pretty darned good neighborhood and it doesn't need a lot of reweaving or improvements. Certain things can be detrimental. One to pick on is the huge increase in density that's proposed for our residential neighborhoods. We are a neighborhood of two and three unit buildings and two and three stories.  This would change the density to what the property owners decide within the [new] bulk and height. To get the six units is pretty easy within those parameters. That's a doubling of the density in our residential neighborhood. That's a point we have a concern about. We look forward to working with you, bringing our points to you and hope you and the staff will be open to the amendments so we can embrace this plan. Peter Cohen I think the schedule of hearings is reasonable if everyone is ready to do a lot of work. I want to make sure that when folks talk about the length of time this has taken there was a significant dead zone for a couple of years while the EIR was being prepared. I don't want there to be a mistake that people feel they need more time. We are starting into a new phase of dialogue. The hearing schedule is reasonable. We are looking at an adoption packet. This is not flipping the pages.  It is reading new materials.  It's the adoption-codified stuff.  It's an experimental plan. Rincon was 12 development projects. This is a neighborhood.  We are prefabricating fragile virtues in the case report. We have to be careful about the fine-tuning process and list to the community who lives there. I think they should be taken seriously. This is about getting it just right. A few quick issues: Mid-block open space - a lot of the development impact in residential neighborhoods happens in the interior of the block.  You don't see it in the street but you feel it when you live there.
it would be great to get a survey of the garage additions.
I'm happy to say a piece of legislation moved yesterday.
Better Neighborhoods Plus provided the structure for the public benefits program. How do you deal with the up zoning included in the plan?
On the Board of Haze Valley Neighborhood Association I'm not speaking for them. Dennis Richards mentioned this was a 30-year plan. I hope it doesn't turn into a 30-year planning process.

I've been involved since 2000 since it started. The Planning Department should be commended for their outreach and the number of community meetings they have done. I'm in support of the plan. I think we need to really move forward as expeditiously as we can. I live a half block off Octavia Boulevard. There are a dozen parcels waiting to be developed. My neighborhood is in limbo.  We are waiting for the plan to go forward before things can be completed on Octavia as well as other sites. We need to consider the plan and the information we have before us. The schedule proposed by the planning staff allows us to do that. I hope we will not delay this plan any further. Tes Wellborn, Haight-Ashbury Council I have participated in the Market/Octavia plan for the past six years and have seen several hundred people participate in that plan. As you move forward, take into account all those people who have been at meeting after meeting. This plan benefits all of San Francisco. We support the plan. But the plan is translated into zoning and community improvement planning. I urge you to have additional meetings besides the public hearings where the details can be worked out. We need to put things in that are not there now that modify some things and move fast at the same time. Hopefully in a couple of months we could have this tied up. Let's get some of these things like affordable housing and the community benefit's plan nailed down more tightly and better. Sue Hestor Looking at your scheduled, hearing number 2 is a killer hearing. One of the unfortunate thing this Commission does is call up the entire calendar. Items 1-6 the only time the public has time to comment is a one three-minutes opportunity on areas on Market Street. There are huge differences in the communities on Market Street and huge difference in the topic items. If you are going to do things right commit yourself that each item is called separately, show you don't' really cheat the public. I think you need to have serious discussions on the backside impact on Imrket Street. You need to see the scale of what is there.  That includes photos. You don't have that now unless you got different things than I did. You really need to see what is the impact where you have large buildings on Market Street and small possibly historic buildings to the rear. Those are the issues I have dealt with over my cases. There needs to be appropriate attention paid to the non-Haze Valley part of this. I don't think it is unusual to say you maybe should have a little bit of explanation on issues particular to neighborhoods that are not the core. Marilyn Amini I feel it is good you will mail to every resident that will be impacted. I'm wondering, will the mailed notice be neighborhood specific? That touches on the question as to how you are going to organize discussions. As Sue mentioned, there is a huge difference in communities and how they are impacted. If you will communicate in your notice area specifically and how those particular areas will be impacted, people will feel they are given adequate notice. Gary Weiss, President, Upper Market Association, EDPA, the CDB and Merchants of Market and Castro. I want to speak as a small business owner in the Castro. I wish I could have participated earlier on. None of the groups I am affiliated with were aware. The main point is parking. We don't feel the point of view of Eureka Valley residents were included.  We need more parking not less. The small businesses in the area are suffering from lack of parking spaces. When large projects are in the works regular information forums are a tool to educating the public. This one, despite the neighbors in the eastern end of the plan, is lacking. We are asking for a delay. This will ensure a large element of the plan area will have the ability to review the plan and input its views.

It was nice seeing those cities, all of which I think are bigger than ours. One of the things we struggle with in the city is the compactness of the city and the interface between tall buildings on one street and there rear yards of the house on the other. They are about to come before the Commission with Market/Octavia. What I didn't see and which we had more of is how to fit the contexts in when you have lots 25 feet wide or 50 feet wide and no big green space around the high rise. They are literally up against the house behind them. It would be nice to struggle through those principles and not have the Boston, Chicago tall buildings where you have the abstract discussions – which are nice – but you deal with the  real world  every Thursday. We all do. If we don't sort it out with Market/Octavia, I don't think we ever will. Unidentified Speaker I was glad to see the presentation and the training going on. Some of those things are missing in the department. What I want the department to think about in green buildings is they have to be in a green block. It has to have transit. We have been patting ourselves on the back by creating the new residential neighborhoods like Rincon Hill and say that everyone is going to walk. They are not. Rincon is a hill. You have to walk up it and we don't have MUNI on that list. Why is it MUNI has had cuts in their service; cut their lines? How can we justify reducing parking and doing green buildings and not at the same time mass transit? MUNI capacity was added to Market Street but it wasn't added to Mission Street. The [number] 14 is a pit. I tell you now; you will have problems on Market Street because people won't be able to get on in all the areas. It's over capacity.

The reason I am here is I was hoping to have Commissioner Hughes here to speak to the issues raised. I am not sure why an informational presentation. I think there is a decision that should be make relative, in light of the presentation the AIA made I think these are concerns that this Commission is taking seriously. In deed if there is redesign, hopefully it does conform and fit with the direction that this Commission seems to be taking. Sue Hestor I want to point out a context issue. This is Harrison Street between Third and Second Streets, right north of the freeway. It's not an attractive walking environment. We are missing the opportunity to look at the context when we do these projects piecemeal like this. This is like an offshoot of Rincon Hill, down two blocks. It's not going to be a pleasant place to walk. They have little street trees in front. Harrison is encroached to the freeway. Cars come down it at a slip. It's a big accident intersection at Harrison and Fourth. When are we going to decide we need to look at what is the context of this site for housing? We are approving a lot of conversions. At a certain level it is easy to do in the North of Market because it is transit [rich]. Do you know what Harrison Street feels to a pedestrian and how isolated you will feel from the north when you come down Fourth Street? It's long blocks and bleak. Are we going to pay attention to that? Put trees in front. That will not solve the entire problem. It may make it worse by darkening the street. It's not an attractive area for pedestrians.

Project Sponsor representative [did not give name]

What we are talking about is a benefit that's conferred on the Sponsor by the Planning Code only if they agree to put the BMR units on site.

By doing that they get a bump in the floor area ratio.

They picked up a little bit of storage space in the basement and a small amount of residential space.

It's to make use of the floor area, which would be dead space in the building.

 This conditional use is encourage by the Planning Code in order to encourage the Sponsor to have the BMR units located on site as opposed to paying an in lieu fee.

Jim Salinas

We have stated this position in the past, we believe the greatest benefit to the city is to have the below market rate units on site as opposed to off site.

 We are not in agreement with in lieu fees.

We believe the City doesn't gain anything by it and the City benefits greater when those below market units are on site.

section: CONSIDERATION OF ITEMS PROPOSED FOR CONTINUANCE
comment: Representing the Project Sponsor on item 10. There is no basis for continuance. The building application is separate from any matters involved in litigation between the builder and the neighbor. If the requestor of the continuance had made their request in a timely fashion they would have heard that it was not granted and would have been prepared. This permit holder has been waiting a long time. It is a minor permit application.  There is little substance. Staff is here and prepared to move forward. I don't believe we should take more staff or commission time with a matter as minor as this. I think we should hear it today and get it over with.

We live in a beautiful city. People come to enjoy the architecture and things that give the City character. I think in general this ordinance may be a good idea. As I read it, or the language I've read so far there are ambiguities. As a person that might apply for a garage permit, I am concerned. It would be nice if the language could be clarified. For example, what gives a building architectural merit? How will the homeowner approach this? The other comment I heard raised was consideration of whether the interior of the space will be altered. You do have to do modification to the front room otherwise you couldn't get the clearance to get your ramp down. I would question what relevance that has to preserving the exterior architectural part of the building. Nobody will come through your house to see the interior as long as it complies with the codes for livable space. I am concerned about the language regarding bay windows. Any alterations to bay windows [shouldn't] be prevented because I rarely see a garage put in where some alteration hasn't been required unless the building is high enough off the ground that you can drive in and it wouldn't create an obstacle. Joe Butler I was here a couple of weeks ago and in looking at the revised draft of the bulletins, some of the things that were mentioned on the September 14 meeting are not here. The issue of affordability, which was discussed by many of the speakers; tenant displacement. I'm wondering if the full commission would like to see some consideration of those items.

Project Sponsor [did not state name]

We will keep it one family with the kids in San Francisco.

This is what your recommendation is – to keep them in San Francisco.

This project is a small 500 square foot addition.

Our main concern is the blockage of sunlight to our kitchen, which is on the south side and there is a bay window that sticks out. We will have minimal light in the kitchen if the proposed project is approved. The sponsor has placed a balcony in that area. It's a clear view to our kitchen and [will cause a] severe lack of privacy and it did not meet our concern to the sunlight in the kitchen. I recommended alternative suggestions. Because the residents concern is not a garage, they can build in that area. They don't have to build a second floor. We want an adequate setback that doesn't block the light from our kitchen. Most kitchens are designed for the most sunlight to enter. We will have minimal if the proposed project is approved. George Sang, Representing the Project Sponsor I have known the family for more than 20 years. They have been living there for 15 years. All these years they have wanted to have a house like everyone else on the block. The house now is less than a thousand square feet. They want another 600 square feet. We feel that we are not asking anything that's not in the neighborhood. Yu Chi Chin When they bought the house, they had not much money. Now that the children are grow-up, she would like to make her house a safe environment to get out of her car to go to the new addition.

representing Dennis McCarthy, DR requestor I live in back to the south of the subject property. The subject property is adjacent to this property, which has been sold. The former owner signed a letter of support; these owners have not signed a letter of support. We object to the proposed three-story building because it's not compatible with the other two-story buildings. This project will affect the adjacent houses.  It is going farther and higher.  It is going 13 feet deeper; and 17 feet deeper to the buildings to the north. We proposed  a two-story building in accordance with their proposal. We proposed a 2-story building.  Downstairs, which has a room that they call an exercise room but looks like an illegal in-law or second unit has a second entrance and a direct connection to the garage that can be converted to an illegal unit by moving this door and moving that door there.  We propose that can be a bedroom and the staircase can descend straight down. We propose the bedroom they renamed a study remain a bedroom; and we propose dining room remain as the dining room and the rear bedroom become a bedroom and bathroom. They will achieve their goal of three bedrooms, four bathrooms with a two-story building. It can be achieved much cheaper than a three-story building and we feel this is a win/win proposal. Karen Mitchell I live on 26 th  Avenue behind the subject property and a little to the north. My topic is the height of the project. The height of the three-story building is not compatible with the neighboring of two-stories in the RH-1 District. The plan to put on a front deck is incompatible with any of the houses Deli Young, Project Sponsor Dennis McCarthy filed DR and he is not here. Karen, I don't believe, lives within the 150-foot radius. In October 2004 and September 2005, we had our first and second out reach meeting to discuss concern about blocked views. On December 22, 2005 we had a third out reach meeting at the request of certain neighbors that claimed their concerns were not being addressed. To address Sheila and Lucy on how the property will fit in the character of the other houses -- these flats are made out of a mix of two and three story houses. The purpose of the front setback incorporate my plans to minimize the impact on the character of the existing block. For Sheila McCarthy concern how the property will affect her privacy and amount of light -- the current subject property plan sufficiently addresses her concerns pertaining to her house. To address Rose and Margaret, they didn't have concerns on how the property will block the ocean view.  It was indicated that we were in our right to expand our property. Karen is outside the 150-foot boundary criteria. The Meeting was adjourned when no one had additional questions or concerns. Today, we are here at the hearing of Discretionary Review because a neighbor is complaining that his concerns regarding my project have not been addressed. The trend you may see is that every time we have a meeting to discuss the concern of the project they come back with more issues to delay the project. I do not think there is anything we can do to satisfy the neighbor.  In other words, they don't want us to build in any manner. I do have a letter of support from the neighbor's house that was sold. Larry I am a 35 years resident on 27 th  Avenue. Much the neighbors to my north have three-story buildings. [Showing a picture] This project is almost on the sidewalk and blocks a significant amount of my light and air. I want to note that the Wong's project does not and I see no reason why it shouldn't go forward.

name_raw: All the paperwork I have seen
comment: All the paperwork I have seen it looks like a lawful project. I don't see how one person can stop another person from their project as long as they follow the guidelines. These neighbors are good neighbors.  They have bent over backwards to conform to the laws of San Francisco and keep to the shape and look of our neighborhood. I am asking you to approve their project. Paul Nazaler I live across the street from the proposed project. I have no problems with this project. It conforms to the Planning Commission and zoning. I hope you will pass an opportunity not to discretionary review it and will approve it. Don Wong, Project designer My brother and sister-in-law asked me to do this project three years ago. Had I known this would happen, I would not drawn the plans up. I did not know it would take three years. We are not talking about building a mansion. They have two kids. I worked with Michael Smith at Planning.  We complied with everything he asked us to do.
Unless you have questions for me, we will await your pleasure

name_raw: Joel Yodowitz, on behalf of Project Sponsor
comment: We want to take over two storefronts on Union Street. Keep the exterior with a new coat of paint and original signage. This proposal will be good for San Francisco residents and the health and convenience of the City by allowing people a full service health club and gym. If would be good for local businesses because it will generate pedestrian traffic on Union Street and promote patronage of near by businesses. No parking is required by the code. We expect most people to walk or take public transit to the gym. The person requesting that this be taken off the consent calendar is a competitor of a very small palates studio. We don't compete with yoga or palates studios. Crunch has weights. It doesn't offer personalized studio type classes like the person who wants this taken off the consent calendar. The concern that Crunch would affect their business is over stated and it shouldn't be a fear. Daron Press I would be the co-owner of the studio that Joel is referring to. My wife and I own Mercury Fitness focusing on palates. It has come to our attention that Crunch is opening a block and a half away from us. There is a focus on small group classes there. There is a Crunch three blocks up the street on Polk and Union. 1500 feet away. For me, I find it hard to believe that crunch would want to open up another so close to another gym. The Union Street [association] prides itself on supporting businesses and tries to stop saturation of formula businesses retail or personal services. This is not an added benefit to the community. There are many fitness facilities in that district that offer the same classes they offer. Parking will be an issue. Our bottom line as well as other small fitness centers will be adversely affected by this place opening up two blocks away. I am asking to protect the small fitness centers by taking their application for conditional use and removing it from the calendar, which we are doing now, and oppose it. 1)

Substantial neighborhood organizations have requested that the Supervisors file of improvements of Eastern Neighborhoods be brought back to the Commission. The legislation sets forth and establishes major planning policy. It's a Better Neighborhood Planning and Implementation legislation that was not recommended by the Committee. You have been told it was not before you and Planning testified in your behalf at the only two Board committee hearings held on the matter. The legislation sets precedence in that it legitimizes its task force concept by codifying it as with the West SOMA Citizens Planning Task Force. The prototype West SOMA Task is politically appointed. Its planning department for planning plans expertise rests in the Planning Department As acknowledged before the Board of Supervisors, the Planning Department acknowledged functioning in advisory capacity to the West SOMA Citizen's Planning Task Force. Important presidencies are being established with this particular piece of legislation, which is up for its final on Tuesday. We strongly request that you bring this back. You have the right to. It's major planning policy. You shouldn't be left out of the loop. There should not be a short circuit to not have you consider these items of major importance. The Brown Act allows you to direct staff to place the item on a future agenda. That is something you could do as action, which is appropriate at the time of Public Comment. I'm pleading. President Alexander Linda, can we send a letter to the Board of Supervisors asking they send this for [our] comment? Commission Secretary Avery It will go out over your signature. None

Representing T-Mobile T-Mobile is intending to install antennas above the Sprint and Cingular antennas It will not interfere with the church. It's considered a preference one location under the City's guidelines. It provides adequate height and visually is un-obstructive. Our report concludes under the emission's guidelines of the San Francisco Public Health Department and FCC that exposure levels are below the [minimum] levels and are less than two percent of the public exposure limit. This installation will allow coverage in the surrounding residential neighborhood. It allows law enforcement and emergency personal to locate and respond to 911 calls from cell phones. A meeting was held and five people attended the meeting.  They were given a brief presentation of the project.  There was no opposition.

Project Engineer The project Sponsor has the support from neighboring business. They are willing to consider a three-year conditional approval of the lot or sooner of the site development plan for approval and implementation. I have a letter from McDonalds [the land owner] and we have a gentleman here to speak on this. Drew Nash I work in the Real Estate Division of McDonalds. We are in the process of negotiating for the re-development of the site. We are working with the franchise at that location in the system to attain an agreement to develop the existing site. We are looking at a two to five year program for re-developing the site. In 1994 it was approved for 144 low-income units for senior citizens. We are looking at a comparable mixed-use development to go in that location. [No name was given] The parking lot next door to McDonalds is fenced up and at night is broken in by the homeless. All they want to do is fix it up and give revenue for the City and parking to the neighborhood. The schools love the idea of the parking.  They can park and be safe instead of it being dark and abandoned. The Commission should approve this as interim parking for two to three years. [Name was not understood] – Liberty Management I believe one of Mr. Li's concerns is that McDonalds Corporation will take their time in terms of starting the project because the developer is coming in from Liberty Park Management. The monthly rent is something close to $3,000 a month. As indicated, it would be a good project in terms of providing a good parking place for people in the neighborhood and for teachers and parents coming to pick up kids from school. If I had my kid in that school I wouldn't want my kid to hang around people using drugs. If you walk the lot you will see needles and garbage in the lot. Even though it is fenced, people get in.

I want to address one absence here under height and bulk; siteing and massing. At all times when we are measuring how tall buildings are, how big they look and how big a bulk to you, you are looking at whether or not it's on a hill, which could make a four-story building look like a seven-story building. You have to address this section. I would like to have that added. I would say that I revised the language of Mr. Nikita's presentation in the case of the corner building he showed early on where the massing is on a corner and you see two facades. It was gracious of him to imply that a variance be considered so it would complete the block face. Then what? A wall everywhere? I don't know if we want that. Corner buildings are a special case. If you have a requirement for rear yard open space there is more coverage allowed by the code. I think it's gratuitous to say to close up an open space viewed to the street. Joe Butler I'm an architect in the city. I think it's a nice presentation, if you are not skilled in the terms or language you would use around town and look and see if you can find examples that do please and delight. I think uniformity and exception could be the 12 th pairing, and in some ways it goes to Maryann's comments in the building law and do we want the entire block wrapped. The exception with the block face can be an inviting and delightful thing. When you are in a part of Russian Hill and the buildings make the street wall in a strong way and you come to a smaller building with gardens and trees, that exception can be something pleasing and delightful.

Had he done the necessary documents and my fears of imminent death and destruction [were addressed], my neighbors and I would not be here. Undermining the stability of the wall or grant sequoia& The wind tunnel necessary& May the commission's common sense prevail before the winds do in its absence of necessary analysis that is germane to the project that caused me consternation& Douglas Gillies and an obscure absentee partner of 461 Chenery named de la Cruz, if they exist, and the contractors of record be held financially responsible to whose homes are damaged. The Gillies are required to post a $3 million dollar bond for ten years from date of construction for the sequoia to be removed [language is not clear]; service elevator, lift garages or crane hoisted over 61 [foot] roof; new tree of same variety to be installed and crater left in yard; the new sequoia over Gilly roof; all destroyed neighboring homes to be built to code. In support of DR [name was not given] I live across the street from the proposed construction site. My concern is parking. In front of 461 there is space for two cars to park now. They are proposing a garage to go in. That will probably remove both off street parking places. They are proposing a two-lift garage in this small building. I think in theory a lift garage is a good idea. In practicality, if there are two lifts, it's a multi-unit building that will house several people. There will be at least four people and they will all have cars. This is not practical at all. I ask the commission to review this and look at that.  And study it because that is not practical to do this. If they build that type of building with those units and have that many tenants in the building, it is due diligence to the owners to provide off-street parking.

Representing the Project Sponsor We are prepared to address the issue raised in the DR request. This is a project consistent with the neighborhood character and guidelines. This is a code complying project. It will add one new housing unit and add 4 more parking spaces to the building where there are presently none. We propose a ten- foot curb cut to get to the parking spaces. One on-street space will be lost.  There will be a net of three spaces added to the neighborhood. You heard from the [DR requestor] that this project was approved in violation of the California Environment Act. This project was exempt as an addition to a single family home because of it's height. It's less than 40 feet; there was no need for a shadow concern. The main complaint is that the vertical addition and the excavation building to the rear yard will damage the tree and pose a risk to the house next door. I would like to point out as far as we know there was no evidence submitted before today. I haven't seen anything from an arborist that there will be damage to the tree. Under California Law, a property [owner] has a right to remove branches or root if it is a reasonable matter. All work will be in due regard for the safety of the neighbor and if possible, without damage to her tree. As Mr. Smith said, we agreed to hire an arborist to evaluate whether or not there will be damage to the tree. If there will be damage, we will replace it with a tree more appropriate to a dense urban environment. Legally, maintaining the tree is the DR applicant's responsibility. The tree is covered in ivy. There are brown leaves on it and it is pushing over the fence. It is a maintenance problem for the sponsor. And it is really something that we could ask the DR applicant to fix, but we agreed to replace the tree if we cause damage to it.

Executive Director of Services We are the project sponsors of 275 10 th  Street.  It is 135 units for homeless adults.  We expect to open in 2008. Our organization has been present in the SOMA since 1894, when our predecessor organization opened a center for immigrants on 2 nd  Street. We have been located on 8 th  Street, which moved there in 1941. We rebuilt that as residences in 1994 and moved to Howard in 1983, and we opened the community house as residents for homeless families. We provide permanent housing with support services for homeless adults and children. This is consistent with the city's ten-year plan to end homelessness and it is key to supportive housing. We are asking your review of the Environmental Impact Report and your approval of the report as accurate and adequate. This is a project in which we partner with the Department of Public Health for services as we do at other sites. We are partnering with the Mayor's Office of Housing. We think it is in the spirit of the SOMA neighborhoods. Bob Hermann, Architect I would like to open by assuring you that the site for this affordable housing does not have a single tree on it.  That may simplify matters. [Laughter] As I understand the purpose is to give you an accurate and broad-brush explanation of what the proposal is about. I'm not going to get into interest detail. I will be happy to answer questions if you have any. [Using slides/renderings, showed the proposed project, its design, and how it functions.] [The Commission President reminded him that the focus of this hearing was to address the environmental document.]

The letter that the Director referred to that was sent to the Board of Supervisors apparently took a while to be delivered. Because here you have 140 people in the Department and a request was made on Thursday by the Commission that is going to be acted upon one way or another by the following Tuesday. The letter gets to the Board on the afternoon on Monday and only gets there because someone in the community hand carries it to the Board of Supervisors. When do you know [think] your request would have been considered if it had been done through the normal distribution process? You need to ask yourself and consider carefully the issue that was raised earlier about how much time does the Commission have to respond to a referral from the Board of Supervisors? The whole battle here is not all about property rights or who's building something and blocking someone's view. The Coalition is coming back and speaking to you about your rights and authority to be exercised under the City Charter to have on all planning issues and matters before you. Here, you have an effort being made by the Board of Supervisors to basically, push everything under the Administrative Code. How long does it take Mr. Sider for the Department to review this? We have is the Department gets 90 days because it is referred by the Board of Supervisors according to the Planning Code. What we are trying to protect is the rights and the authority and responsibility of the Planning Commission to conduct its business so the public can proceed to help and provide the support in the public process. Ms. Espanola Jackson I want to speak on the Supervisor's meeting that occurred last Tuesday. This was without Committee reference. That is how you get things done behind your back. Because they did not want it to be hard by you or the community. It was item 31. I know because one of the residents that was there had to be pulled by Supervisor Maxwell. And it was read. And you know what it was? It has to do with eminent domain on 2 acres of land. Please, do not be passing on things that have not been heard by the community or you because she says so. You got the responsibility. It's not up to her to make the decision for you and the entire City. Tony Kelly I wanted to speak in reference to the comments of the others about what happened on Tuesday. It seems that this is a property issue. No one can do anything before talking to Planning first. It was done properly. It is for the Supervisors to consider. It was discussed at the Planning Commission. Yet there are individuals from the Coalition of San Francisco Neighborhoods that say it's not enough. My association is a member of the Coalition. It was not brought to my association or brought to anyone in the Eastern Neighborhoods. If they have a campaign of their own, it's these three individuals doing it themselves. They don't represent the Coalition or the Southern or Eastern Neighborhoods who need this legislation and more. Francisco DA Costa I belong to the San Francisco Coalition of Neighborhoods. I participated in all the planning workshops regarding the Eastern Neighborhoods. This matter came before the Coalition as an emergency, because that way it was sneaked in. It was in a bad way. All I'm saying if you want to bring certain types of amendments, or certain types of policies linked to the Administrative Code, then we need to have a public discussion. These types of policies are sneaked in on a fast track and sent to the Board of Supervisors. We, the constituents, do not have a say. It is wrong for people to say this doesn't pertain to the Eastern Neighborhood. We have the right to introduce any type of amendments and legislations through our process within the Coalition. No name Thank you for your action requesting an important plan on land use issues authored by Supervisors be sent back to you. I am sad by the Board of Supervisors action on last Tuesday, in response to your request for return of file 61206. I feel in particular that Supervisor McGoldrick's remarks were questionable. He said that the planning issue comes back for your hearing and response. That was the Eastern Neighborhood's policy and rezoning and community planning matter. Supervisor McGoldrick reported to all Supervisors present, that the Planning Director and Zoning Administrator were in support of the community legislation. Judy Berkowitz I would like to tell you that the Coalition for San Francisco Neighborhoods unanimously passed two resolutions at our meeting on Tuesday. The second one I think that you have not been briefed on was that we urged the veto of the ordinance to the Mayor and that the Board refer it to the Planning Commission for your comment and review. My husband and I are the requestors. We live next door and have lived there for 22 years and were happy until the time we had the backyard flooded because of heavy rain. It's never a pleasant experience to wade in cold water in winter to drain buckets of water. In June, when we found the owners plan on extending 20 feet in the rear, we were very upset. If our yard were as long as theirs, we would have no problem with that length. Unfortunately our yard is short. The project would leave not enough space for good air to circulate. In order to allow our neighbors to expand and to have less negative impact on us the best solution would be to modify the project plan. We suggest two modifications: 1) setback the south wall 6-1/2 feet on both levels. This will allow them to keep their existing door downstairs and the door upstairs; 2) keep the length to 14 feet. This length matches the adjacent property's extension and is in tune with the neighborhood. With this extension the project owner would have a huge master bedroom of 14 x 18 and 1⁄2 feet. If the project is not setback on the ground floor, we would feel devastated from our second floor window. We would look at a wall and a dirty roof. Jeffrey Chin The sponsor is willing to listen to the recommendations of the staff. We were willing to reduce it, give it a 3 foot setback on the south side and setback 5 feet as staff requires and install windows on the second floor six feet from the floor in accordance with staff's request. The project sponsor needs more space. The belief is that the addition is not taking up all of the space he could take. The issue they have with the flooding on the side that's a structural issue and has nothing to do with the planning and the plans being proposed. The construction will be done so the rain comes out of the rear of the house. Mike Chan My brother, my sister, and my parents have lived in this house since the 90's. It is a 2-bedroom house. We were cramped. Now that I am married and have a baby with us, we are even more cramped for space. We can't afford to buy anything in the City.

Our family came to San Francisco in the 1880;s and they fell in love with this country and wanted to stay. They struggled for many years and during World War II they lost everything they had to build it back again. It was with great sacrifices and work and dedication that they are able to build themselves to the level they are and be able to purchase a home in San Francisco. They were not allowed to rent or buy homes in certain areas of the City back then. I don't think it was City law. It was exclusionary. A social injustice. They chose that home because it's a peaceful place. We will loose our light and view and privacy on that side of the house if their project is able to build up on the third level. I wish we could some how figure a way out where we could both be happy. I suggested they build in the front of their house, so they can get the same new area in their home, as if they built the penthouse there and it will not interfere with my view, privacy, light and space. No name Former speaker is my sister and we both live in the house. I would like to say the decision to come forward was not an easy one for her or me. It was really difficult for us. We are not confrontational people and we struggled with this. We didn't want to cause waves or step on anyone's toes. We really did try to consider whether we could live with this addition so close to us. The proposed extension is tall - almost 13 feet vertical elevation of the existing structure. It would block a good portion of the direct light entering our bedroom and block entirely our view of Lincoln Park Golf Course. In addition, we would be loosing the privacy we enjoy in our home and backyard with the neighbors boarding our property. In San Francisco the open space and privacy is relished and it's a treasure. Jonathan, Architect for the project Gave a brief description of the project. Michael Saksteder, Project Sponsor We like our neighborhood and neighbors and tried hard to be sensitive to everybody's needs, while still getting what we thought we could get out of what we think is a modest project. We were sensitive to our neighbor's needs in the planning and design of the project and in the approval process of the project. We oriented the project so it was angled such that it didn't block the views of our neighbor. We did not build it as large as it could have been because we didn't want to disrupt or impact the neighborhood. In the approval process we tried to make sure we got the entire neighborhood input we could. It's at a point now where it's significantly delaying our project to be asking for input on the project when we provided opportunity for that input some significant time ago. I also think that the privacy concern that's been raised is not an issue. We are trying to be good neighbors and we have tried to do the project right. Bryan Eckert I live at 259 32 nd Avenue across from the subject property. I am in full support of the proposed project. I think it's an enhancement to the neighborhood.

Hope Net is a good cannabis facility. They have served our City and their neighborhood well. Much before the existence of Hope Net, the energy that Steve and Kathy Smith have brought to the medical cannabis community says great things about these two individuals and this facility. They have put together a wonderful staff that understands the needs of the patients. This should be approved. It is in the best interest of our community and the best interest of the City. Michelle Aldrich I am speaking for Hope Net. It is one of the model dispensaries for the whole City. Steve and Kathy are great people. A lot of the patients live in Section 8 housing, and they can't medicate at home. These people feel safe at Hope Net. The whole neighborhood feels safer because Hope Net is there I hope you will vote for it. Richard Muller I met Steve and Kathy a year and a half ago. Since then, I have gone to their facility. Before we had access to go to Hope Net we met a group, the Patients Health Defense Union. A lot of us were poor, the prices of normal clubs were above what we could afford for our medicine. Rose Kenyon I am a medical cannabis patient. I've been in this area for 40 plus years and have been prescribed many different types of medications for the health issues that I have. I find that medical marijuana is best for me. I feel that since we have voted to have medical marijuana in the City, it's almost a travesty and a slap in the face that we have to deal with issues that are outside of being able to medicate at any time. These dispensaries are being eliminated. They are well established and reputable and not fly-by-night establishments. They do give compassion. And in our language that is no cost medication or little cost. I recommend that you take the proposal of your staff. John Caldera I am a United States Navy Veteran and a California card-carrying member and I have lived with HIV since November of 1995. Medical cannabis has helped keep me alive. I am here to speak on behalf of Hope Net, which is a phenomenal dispensary. They have done a lot for the community. I ask you to allow them to continue the services to so many patients in the community. Terrie Frye I'd like to say that I am grateful to Kathy and Steve Smith for the priorities of the Hope Net dispensary and for their donations to me. I have been able to quit taking medicine for depression, which didn't work anyway. I am not taking them anymore and I am not depressed. The only thing that would depress me now is if you didn't permit them to stay open. Rev. Randi Webster Hope Net is a model facility through compassion and community awareness and their striving to be better in helping patients. They care for their patients and open their doors to everyone. Please, do not take discretionary review. They are doing a fine job. Cathy Smith I am the owner and operator of Hope Net We are here to hopefully obtain the community's consent to operate. It's our goal to continue our compassion program to the terminally ill and we want to help as many as we can. We would like to thank the businesses and the community for their support and we would like to thank you people, the Planning Commission. We really have been a community minded organization. We would like to continue to be an organization that can service the community and we want you to let us keep operating and helping these nice people in San Francisco. Johnny Nolen When I became involved with the medical cannabis community, I realized I was helping the direct needs of the patients by obligating myself to a political movement to protect the rights of the patients. I met caregivers and listened to different people on how we can be integrated into San Francisco. I was impressed by their services and professionalism and community awareness. Hope Net helps San Francisco's largest compassion program by supplying medicine to severely ill patients. This is an important precedence to set with no insurance covered medical cannabis. Shona - Executive Director of a patient advocacy organization. I am nervous out of excitement that our City can be a model for the nation. We believe that Hope Net co-op should be a statement and standard for all to follow in this process, because of their unbelievable compassion program. We want permitted low impact costs for people with fixed income. They offer their space to the Women's Health Collective and other community groups. I believe the permitting of this compassionate co-op in San Francisco becoming the model for the nation. Leslie Thomas I am a patient that uses medical marijuana. I have gone to Hope Net on 9 th Street in order to obtain my medicine since they first opened. I feel comfortable going to Hope Net because they have made a conscious effort to make the neighborhood a clean and safe environment. My experience with Hope Net has been from a patient's perspective instead of a customer. I am treated like a patient not as a customer. My needs have been valued with compassion toward a patient. Your consideration to allow Hope Net to remain at their current location will be much appreciated. Robert Carlton I am here to speak in support of Hope Net. I have been a patient and also associated with them for as long as they have been open. They are the most compassionate club in San Francisco. Tony Bowles I am a neighbor to Hope Net. I run a bookstore next door. I have seen how, since Hope Net opened, that element in that location is reduced. I would like to say that patients and supporters in San Francisco united in the face of losing everything have fought hard to protect – a patient's right to legally obtain medical cannabis. In closing I would like to say, give medical cannabis a chance. Give Hope Net a chance. Michael Aldrich Hope Net has been there for three years with no complaints. It has met all the requirements of the new regulations. They are taking care of a hundred patients, absolutely free. It's a historical building. They spent sums of money to make it accessible. This will be the first medical cannabis dispensary approved by the Planning Commission. Dana Blackford I have sustained brain injury in my life, which has lead to my inability of accomplishing many things. The fact that I started using cannabis has alleviated many of my stresses. I would think it would be frivolous of you to close them down. Jim Meko Isn't it a blessed relieved that unlike the last time you took DR on a medical cannabis club that this is so much more positive of an experience? We don't have this divisiveness between those complaining with the drugged criminal element on the one hand and the belittling yuppies on the other hand. I ask strongly that you approve this permit as recommended by staff. Bruce Allison Please give these guys a chance. They run a clean and decent dispensary.

name_raw: Dean Preston, Director of Tenants Together
comment: -- a statewide organization for tenant's rights. We are perusing fairness and justice for California's 14 million Tenants. In February we are launching a foreclosure rights hotline for tenants around the state to call because so many tenants and organizations that serve tenants are in the dark about this. Tenants are innocent victims of the foreclosure crisis. They are living in property and they are not the ones who are not paying the mortgage – they are presumably the ones who are paying their rent and then a foreclosure occurred. In 2008 there were nearly a quarter of a million foreclosure sales in California. That is more than double the figure for 2007. That just relates to residential. Although the figure is hard to pinpoint, the best estimate is that at least 25% of those properties foreclosed on in 2008 are tenant occupied properties - not owner occupied. The percentage of people impacted by the foreclosures is much higher – closer to 38%. The reason is that many of the buildings that get foreclosed on are multi unit buildings. In San Francisco the numbers are similar. Based on the data we got from a service called Foreclosure Radar, there were 608 residential foreclosures –more than double the number in 2007 and the percentage was 28% that were not owner occupied. These numbers don't capture situations that don't go through a foreclosure sale like a notice of default or situations where a property is deeded back to the lending institution. So the scope of impact on San Francisco and California is much bigger than what the actual foreclosure numbers will show. The affect on tenants varies considerably both around the state and in San Francisco. The most common things we here about are calls about how the property is managed after foreclosure or efforts to evict. Generally the bank is the owner after foreclosure. Either the bank is a very bad landlord or they simply don't want to be landlords. It is common to have no maintenance on the property, no repairs done, utility bill aren't paid and utilities are cut off, and all of this with very little notice to the tenant. On the eviction front, the banks ordinarily move to evict the tenant in the building if they can. In San Francisco has just cause eviction protection for many of its units. In those properties where the rent ordinance applies, a foreclosure is not grounds to evict. Those tenants should be protected. The problem is that many of those tenants don't know that and many of the banks that assume ownership of those properties don't know that. It is important to make sure that all parties involved understand that the change of ownership does not mean that these tenants have to vacate. For those tenants that do have to vacate – those that are not protected by the rent ordinance, perhaps because they are in newer buildings, would have 60 days under a state law passed last year, to vacate the property. Multiple agencies have been involved in this. The Assessors Office has taken a leadership role in moving forward to try to notify the tenant as early as possible – as soon as the notice of default is filed so that these tenants know that they don't have to vacate and that they have certain rights once a foreclosure occurs. Sarah Short, Executive Director of the Housing Rights Committee of San Francisco – We provide counseling and legal information to renters. Over the last year we have definitely have seen a steady increase in the number of cases. The types of issues that people are facing even with just cause protection are situations where landlords disappear. Tenants aren't necessarily aware that the property has been foreclosed on and that the property has changed hands. It may now be owned by a band who has a broker representing them and there are now layers of ownership and just a lack of tenant awareness of who and where to go to for what; where to pay the rent. It's sort of MIA (missing in action) landlord situation. Related to that the brokers or realtors are sort of the middle man are advising tenants much more heavy handedly and demanding that tenants vacate their property; that the building is no longer going to be a rental property. We've seen notes left on doors. We've seen a broker knocking on the door late at night or early in the morning telling people that the building has been foreclosed and you've got to go. This is the first time people have heard of sometimes. One of the things we are most concerned about right now is utility shut offs. The previous owner stops paying the bill and no has taken responsibility to pay the bill and the utilities get turned off. Residents go to PG&E. PG&E tells them how do we know you live there? Or they are told we can set up an account in your name but you are responsible for the back bill. All sorts of things are happening for people without utilities. The other thing we are seeing with these brokers and banks, sometimes banks that are not even in San Francisco, is that they are not aware of our laws here. They have not done their due diligence to find out their responsibility as a landlord now that they officially own that property. They are simply trying to evict people in spite of the fact that it is illegal in San Francisco. A lot of tenants have just seen the notice and they don't know their rights. They are scared and they leave anyway. The other thing that happens is they have to go through the court process and seek agencies that will assist them. They spend a lot time and energy. They build up a lot an anxiety around the future of their home although the bank is doing something illegal. We are just one of several organizations in San Francisco trying to help. We have seen close to a hundred cases this year. We look back two years ago where we saw one case or none. We have formed a coalition with other organizations to work on these issues. One of our first steps was to meet with the Assessors Office and explain that we needed access to the information about who was getting foreclosed on, who the real new owner is, and the renters need to know what is going on so they can assert their rights. The result of that is that the Assessor is going to put out a letter to all residents of foreclosed properties or where a notice of default has been filed that tells them what their rights are and that they do not have to move under San Francisco Rent Control laws, and that have resources, like our organization, to get support. It will also tell them where to go if their PG&E has been shut off, and that they can call the Assessor's Office for help to find out whom to pay the rent to, who is responsible for repairs; who is to held accountable? Some steps we are looking forward to include more work insuring that PG&E does not shut off power in the first place. I note that we do not have this problem with water because it is a public utility and there has been a long standing policy that there is not going to be water shut off in this same type of way. We are also working the City Attorney's Office on trying to enforce some of the state laws to force PG&E to comply. That is one of the biggest problems because when there is no power it can work as an eviction tool. Renters end up leaving the property because it is unlivable and there are displacements. You have an eviction without going through the courts process. We need to figure out a way to protect those tenants that fall through the cracks better. We also need to notify the banks and or lenders. Some of them just don't understand that they are now landlords and they need to know what our laws are and what their responsibilities are. It's mainly an issue of outreach and education to banks, landlords, brokers, utility companies and also to the residents themselves. Sue Hestor – We have a unique situation - condo foreclosures. We have several thousand units of use-restricted condos, namely artist occupancy and live/work. Who is going to pay attention that the occupancy restrictions are enforced? The Planning Department should get ahead of this and include a question on every application of any sort that comes in: Is this owner occupied or a tenant? Commercial properties should be included. We should also start looking at where the tenant doesn't get notice. CUs and Tenants-in-common are examples. We need to get ahead of the blight issue. Those are commitments that we made and my letter does go into detail as to how that commitment is being fulfilled. We feel absolutely 100% sure that we are fulfilling that commitment and all of the work on the job site is being done with union signatory subcontractors. THD is very excited about this project at Pier 15 and 17. We do have concerns about the design of the project and the adequacy and accuracy of the DEIR to describe and consider several important environmental impacts. There are no detailed drawings of the proposed structure of the bridge building in the DEIR that clearly show the materials, architectural details or scaled height measurements in comparison to the historic pier sheds. Some of the proposed materials are incompatible with the historic resources of piers 15 and 17 and the National Register Historic District. Those would include the glass curtain wall system on the east and west façades, and the glass bridges. We are also concerned about the height and bulk of the bridge building. We want to understand why the mechanical apparatus room needs to be in the bridge building causing it to extend further north into the view corridor between the piers. Also, the three possible restaurants totaling 17,000 square feet in piers 15 and 17 which could be consolidated and located so as to reduce the mass and height of the bridge building. How does the design of the proposed bridge building including glass and steel material is necessary to meet the needs of the Exploratorium?
