I'm here on behalf of the June family. I hope this will be the simplest matter you deal with today, the removal of an unsound single-family home that is being replaced by a single-family home to house a six-member family. This is an unsound building based on the conditions of the wood and termites. It's a modest home in a modest area. I think it's appropriate. I don't have anything further to add.

I am co-owner of 479 Arkansas Street, adjacent to 20 th Avenue. The best way for me to describe our issue and for each one of you to experience the situation would be if you owned solar panels and your neighbor puts up a structure that would block the sun - the source of energy for the panels. I paid $20,000 for the panels and they worked. You felt that since the State of California provided funding for these panels you would be protected by California Civil Code 801.5 with provisions to receive sunlight and creating an easement for a solar system. The planner says there is no such code to protect city residents. They say it's a private matter between us. I am here to see whether this Commission can find a way to get someone to be responsible, just as a City wants their documents signed by professionals. Our request is that the project does not obstruct the sunlight. They can be made of transparent materials. It's a roof deck in the most sunny part of San Francisco. I would add, in the magnitude of what we were arguing here, we failed to determine that there are issues of security as a result of the stairway. It comes close to a landing to our bathroom window. There could be someone who could jump from the landing to our property. Margaret Healy, Owner 1640 20 th Street. When he first approached me about the concern of his solar panels I told my architect to look at it. She presented a shadow analysis. It showed a minimal impact on the shadowing. They refused to accept this report and required us to prepare a full calendar year study and financial analysis of how much it would cost in terms of lost energy. I hired 2 solar experts. I made significant design changes. Ripping off the top of my roof and adding $30,000 dollars to the cost of the construction. The design changes were successful. The solar reports only showed a few dollars a year impact on the solar system. They are refusing to accept the results of the report they requested. At this point we've spent five months and $40,000 in reports, design and construction changes. I think we have done enough. I hope the Commission will see we have acted in good faith and as good neighbors.

Council Representative of the Project Sponsor

We work on a lot of historic buildings and this is one of the most interesting historic structures I have dealt with.

When we entered into this with this building it was obvious that 1 Kearny was the historic building and the annex has less historic merit.

When we discovered there was a debate on whether or not it was historic, the owners of the building decide to preserve the building.

The design went through two extensive hearings at the Landmark's Board where there was a divergence of opinion.

Some say the annex should be torn down.

We changed the design in response to the comments made by the Landmark's Board.

You see a design that received unanimous support by the board.

It's an improved design based on a long dialogue with the Planning staff and the Landmark's Board on how to treat a building that is the average landmark restoration project.

Charles, Architect for the project

This is a very important building at an important location in San Francisco.

It is in the Kearney/Market Conservation District, at a very important corner in the city.

 Where one of San Francisco's grids intersects on Market Street.

It's a dramatic building especially seen from Third Street as you approach the city.

There are three parts:

 The original 1902 Savings Bank in the building, which is an early quake survivor, and the annex added in '64.

We planned to tear down the three-story build seen on left in the picture and replace it with a 10-story building.

Our design is an attempt to fill in the missing tooth to Market Street.

We are sensitive to the urban design and context as well as to the specific design itself.

One Kearny and bank annex function as one building.

There are a number of functional problems.

The annex has elevators, stairs and bathrooms.

It is difficult to divide the building into floors.

There is no air conditioning or heat in the annex.

One of our objectives is to correct the functional problems.

The building has a seismic prospect.

 Even though it was an earthquake survivor, it has a stiff element that makes it twist during an earthquake.

Our project will correct all of the functional problems by creating a new core in the new building.

 We'll take the elevators out of the annex.

 We'll make their front door their back door.

We want to put the building in architectural balance.

We are changing brick to glass.

We are using traditional materials like terra cotta in contemporary ways.

We don't have open space on the ground floor; we are proposing to put it on the roof at the top.

name_raw: Paul Wane, Architect for the project
comment: The previous use was a bathhouse. This building has been vacant for 15 years. It's a 3-story building, 11,000 sq. ft. with a 3,500 sq. ft. basement. The height of the building is 46 feet. The taller building to the east of our project is about 69 feet and the smaller building is about 35 feet. For our project, we are proposing that we do a full restoration of the existing historical façade with the new residential and commercial entries at the street level. We are doing a full seismic retrofit of the existing building along with the addition. The two floors added at the rear of the building create a 5-story building with one level of basement. The three off-street parking spaces are actually below grade and accessed via car lift. We are proposing commercial office spaces at the ground level and nine market-rate residential condominiums on floors 2 through 5 with open space on the roof. The height of the addition we are proposing is 19 feet above the existing building. We are adding this portion with the additional 9 feet for various mechanical stairs and elevator penthouses to access the roof. The new building would have a height of 65 feet and the top of the penthouse is approximately 74 feet 6 inches. The break down of the rental units is four one-bedroom studio sized units, three two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units at the top two floors. Our challenge in this project in maintaining the historical façade was how do we bring light and air into the residential units? We have come up with a scheme where we create this large unit court and basically create two rental towers on either side to get light and air into the rental units. There is also a smaller light wall we are cutting in at the back of the building to get light and air in to the deeper units. Also, as the light wall is steep, we are removing a portion of the existing wall and then putting in property line windows looking over that shorter building. Last November we had a meeting with two neighborhood groups – The Tenderloin Collaborative and the North of Market Planning Coalition. Last month we had a follow up meeting with the groups and we didn't get objections. We had a pre-application meeting with the Building and Fire Department because the exiting through the project was tricky to get around. We worked out those issues along with the property line window issues with the Fire and Building Departments. We believe that this project would improve the neighborhood in that it provides nine additional rental units.

I live around the corner from the project. The reason I brought this discretionary review up is the neighborhood and various neighbors have been working for three years to try to come up with a compromise for this particular lot. We feel that this option as well as the previous one that was first submitted in 2003 does not keep in context with the neighborhood. It is much higher than most of the other buildings. It is much bigger, much bulkier and has a very small yard. This particular project site, being a corner lot that is about 62 feet wide by 80-some feet long is large enough to accommodate a variety of different options that would not require a variance or any kind of special considerations. There is plenty of opportunity for designs to have been put forth that would have not required any kind of special considerations. I feel that if a typical resident of San Francisco were trying to make these types of changes and ask for these variances they probably wouldn't be granted very easily. This project sponsor has been all along the way getting a lot to support from the Planning Department, even though the neighbors have been against it for the most part. Although as mentioned there are letters in support, there are also quite a few letters in opposition to this. It's been a three-year battle. I also want to comment on the design and context of this building. I went through the Residential Design Guidelines and found 10 different issues where this building did not meet them (which I have outlined in my discretionary review). A lot of them have to do with the scale, size and context, but also about the design. I think this neighborhood in San Francisco deserves a building more in context with its neighbors and I hope you agree. Roland Salvato I live at 3924 Larkin Street. The reason I'm here is because for the last two and a half years I've been trying to figure out exactly what the logic is and justification for allowing that building to have variances. What's so special about this building that it requires a variance to allow an undersized yard, extensive height and a really bizarre design? If you look at the profile of the building, it's well over 40 feet in some places, as high as 47 feet. It is competing with the Ghirardelli Square Tower across the street. Bradford Whitaker When I first saw the drawing of this new building, I thought, you know, there are some wonderful compromises made by all parties that bothered redesigning this building. We feel that this corner elevation has a discrepancy of over a foot from the prior design and I'd like to know really where the cornerstone is, because it's relative to the total elevation of this property. I'd like to know before you make a determination on what the right elevation for this property is that you've looked into it. As far as height variance or allowable height variances, I'm totally against that. I feel there's too much magnitude here. This building would be kind of a monolithic piece. Jill Bittner I am really frankly shocked that we are still talking about this issue two and a half to three years after the fact. This is right by Ghirardelli Square, ground zero for tourists. This is something that is so flagrantly wrong. It's obvious it's too tall. It's got too big of a footprint. It is out place and out of scale with the neighborhood. Erica Whittaker I just don't understand and why we can't put a building there that will coincide with what else exists there. To me, I think we are an old neighborhood and should be considered a historic neighborhood. Our home just turned 80 years old. Our neighbors are just with us and I would like to see something that looks like it's been there for a hundred years and fits in. Joel Yodowitz, Representing the Project Sponsor What you have before you today is the redesign that expressly agreed to at a meeting with the DR requestors and some of the neighbors.. When listening to the DR requestor, I'd like to remind you that this same DR requestor who requested that the soils be tested a couple of years ago, opposed a demolition permit for this property and the purpose of the demolition permit was to remove the building to do the very soil testing the DR requestor asked for. They appealed this to the Board of Appeals, one of you was on the Board at that time, and the DR request was denied so the soils could be tested. There were countless meetings. representing Project Sponsor We have been working on this project for about four years with the Planning Department.  The Sponsor and I am pleased to be back here today to present the project and its evolution so that maybe we can take you into the mind of the architect and the planners as we come with a proposal that you are going to see here today. I'd like to begin first with the origins of this project and its location.  As you can see from the image on the screen where you see the label, it sits at the intersection of Market and 8 th  Streets and all the way to Mission Street is the current proposed site. For those in the audience who may not be familiar, it is on Market Street directly across from the Orpheum Building, a very well known corridor. The site is currently occupied by the original motel building or hotel building that existed on the site, a horizontal low rise building that is largely surrounded by parking lots. As you can see, there is an anomaly on the site in the fact that Stevenson does not actually traverse that parcel.  When the hotel was built, Stevenson must have been vacated and the parcel was consolidated all the way across. You will see how we respond to that unusual circumstance in the City structure. The existing building occupies most of the length of the site along 8 th. What you can see along the top of the page is how Stevenson actually dead-ends abruptly with no termination cul-de-sac or any other means of return. The site receives the sun from the South and of course east and west at certain time of the day.  And we just show you where the shadows are cast internally with the site. The diagram that is now on the screen is the shadow plan that actually cuts through the site that is truly the true limiting factor, because it really dominates above the zoning heights that are permitted on the site. It becomes really the deciding factor in the massing of the building.  The shadow ordinance requires this and, as you can see, there is a high point on Mission Street that cascades gently along the corner to 8 th  and along Market and eventually to the low corner of Market and 8 th , which becomes the lowest point of the property. But in fact, it's sort of coincidental, it sort of fits into the City texture and the fact that buildings along Market are above the height that the shadow ordinance provides and buildings along Mission, they are evolving; they are quite a bit taller. So, this takes us to the actual site plan of this project and you can see what we are doing fundamentally here, we are trying to reestablish the City grid and reestablish some of the traffic patterns in a coherent way. The axis of Stevenson is reinstated with a pedestrian promenade that takes one directly across the site. What we are actually recreating here is the two original sites with a larger site along Market and a narrower site along Mission. The dead end is extended along the site and makes a regular turn and exits along Mission far enough from the corner so it is a logical intersection at the termination of what Stevenson's is today, which is essentially a service drive. Director of Tenderloin Housing Three years ago when we heard about the project that was planned to demolished at Trinity Plaza, it led to great concern among the tenants and groups like ours because we were going to lose 360 units of rent controlled housing. In response to that threat, I asked Supervisor Chris Daly to introduce legislation to prevent the demolition citywide. Early in December we were planning to re-circulate a special election for June 2005. The end result was that I got a call from Jack Davis, representing Angelo Sangiacomo, who said we've been fighting so long, what if we save all your rent-controlled housing? Well, keep in mind nowhere in the history of California, I don't believe anywhere in the history of America, has anyone built new housing under rent control. They might have build it under Federal, but not under rent control. Of course, State law forbids rent control in new housing. Angelo was suggesting that he would agree voluntarily with a deed restriction for rent control and that all housing would be replaced on site and none of our tenants in the building would be displaced because the minute the building was ready they would move right over. In fact in a subsequent agreement negotiated by Supervisor Daly, the builders are going to pay for the move and the tenants can take all their furniture to the new place as well. That assurance made a big difference. It looked like we could work out something that would be that rare opportunity for people who have been historic adversaries to come together. After all we've said about him [Mr. Sangiacomo], I'm willing to step forward and make peace. If we did the 15% affordable, we would end up with 275 affordable units in this project. Instead we are getting 350 rent controlled units. When you say you could work out a better deal, how come no better deal has ever come? Who could afford to build rent controlled?  Where would they get financing? The truth is if you do not have the wealth of Angelo Sangiacomo, this project wouldn't happen. There is no public money in this. Trinity is giving up 200 commercial parking spaces it already has.  Remember when you take away parking spots from revenue it is already getting, that means that you are taking millions of dollars out of the project.

we could have given up rent controlled units and gotten more affordable units. The tenants opted for more rent control rather than have more affordable units. We would respectfully request that we not be required to do that. 12% affordable [in addition to the rent controlled] was the understanding of the parties – the tenants and Angelo Sangiacomo. We talked with Chris Daly last week and it was not their intent to capture Trinity. There was some discussion about changing the definition of the existing tenant.  We have agreed to that.  We agreed that an existing tenant will be anybody at Trinity Plaza with a lease on the day of the first Certificate of Occupancy or Temporary Certificate of Occupancy. Somebody is suggesting that the north-south pathway between Mission and Stevenson through the private open space be open to the public. We can't agree to that and hope you won't make us agree to it. We have a great big public plaza area.  It's the way it was designed.  We expect the building to be mapped with restrictions subject to City Attorney review. We are going to waive the Ellis Act, waive restrictions.  There is no way that will be sold as condominiums. We understand some accommodations were made not to shadow 1160 Mission, but we are very concerned about how this project treats the public realm; what it does to Market Street; what it does to Mission Street; and what it does to 8 th  Street. Director of Tenderloin Housing Three years ago when we heard about the project that was planned to demolished at Trinity Plaza, it led to great concern among the tenants and groups like ours because we were going to lose 360 units of rent controlled housing. In response to that threat, I asked Supervisor Chris Daly to introduce legislation to prevent the demolition citywide. Early in December we were planning to re-circulate a special election for June 2005. The end result was that I got a call from Jack Davis, representing Angelo Sangiacomo, who said we've been fighting so long, what if we save all your rent-controlled housing? Well, keep in mind nowhere in the history of California, I don't believe anywhere in the history of America, has anyone built new housing under rent control. They might have build it under Federal, but not under rent control. Of course, State law forbids rent control in new housing. Angelo was suggesting that he would agree voluntarily with a deed restriction for rent control and that all housing would be replaced on site and none of our tenants in the building would be displaced because the minute the building was ready they would move right over. In fact in a subsequent agreement negotiated by Supervisor Daly, the builders are going to pay for the move and the tenants can take all their furniture to the new place as well. That assurance made a big difference. It looked like we could work out something that would be that rare opportunity for people who have been historic adversaries to come together. After all we've said about him [Mr. Sangiacomo], I'm willing to step forward and make peace. If we did the 15% affordable, we would end up with 275 affordable units in this project. Instead we are getting 350 rent controlled units. When you say you could work out a better deal, how come no better deal has ever come? Who could afford to build rent controlled?  Where would they get financing? The truth is if you do not have the wealth of Angelo Sangiacomo, this project wouldn't happen. There is no public money in this. Trinity is giving up 200 commercial parking spaces it already has.  Remember when you take away parking spots from revenue it is already getting, that means that you are taking millions of dollars out of the project.

There are several hundred parking spaces that are going in next-door that will be short-term and I think you read the article in the Chronicle on Monday. It also depends on close parking availability in the immediate environment. Most of our shows are at night with 8:00 starts. representing Project Sponsor We have been working on this project for about four years with the Planning Department.  The Sponsor and I am pleased to be back here today to present the project and its evolution so that maybe we can take you into the mind of the architect and the planners as we come with a proposal that you are going to see here today. I'd like to begin first with the origins of this project and its location.  As you can see from the image on the screen where you see the label, it sits at the intersection of Market and 8 th  Streets and all the way to Mission Street is the current proposed site. For those in the audience who may not be familiar, it is on Market Street directly across from the Orpheum Building, a very well known corridor. The site is currently occupied by the original motel building or hotel building that existed on the site, a horizontal low rise building that is largely surrounded by parking lots. As you can see, there is an anomaly on the site in the fact that Stevenson does not actually traverse that parcel.  When the hotel was built, Stevenson must have been vacated and the parcel was consolidated all the way across. You will see how we respond to that unusual circumstance in the City structure. The existing building occupies most of the length of the site along 8 th. What you can see along the top of the page is how Stevenson actually dead-ends abruptly with no termination cul-de-sac or any other means of return. The site receives the sun from the South and of course east and west at certain time of the day.  And we just show you where the shadows are cast internally with the site. The diagram that is now on the screen is the shadow plan that actually cuts through the site that is truly the true limiting factor, because it really dominates above the zoning heights that are permitted on the site. It becomes really the deciding factor in the massing of the building.  The shadow ordinance requires this and, as you can see, there is a high point on Mission Street that cascades gently along the corner to 8 th  and along Market and eventually to the low corner of Market and 8 th , which becomes the lowest point of the property. But in fact, it's sort of coincidental, it sort of fits into the City texture and the fact that buildings along Market are above the height that the shadow ordinance provides and buildings along Mission, they are evolving; they are quite a bit taller. So, this takes us to the actual site plan of this project and you can see what we are doing fundamentally here, we are trying to reestablish the City grid and reestablish some of the traffic patterns in a coherent way. The axis of Stevenson is reinstated with a pedestrian promenade that takes one directly across the site. What we are actually recreating here is the two original sites with a larger site along Market and a narrower site along Mission. The dead end is extended along the site and makes a regular turn and exits along Mission far enough from the corner so it is a logical intersection at the termination of what Stevenson's is today, which is essentially a service drive. [He continued to use his power point slide presentation to describe the existing site and proposed project.]

Director of Tenderloin Housing Three years ago when we heard about the project that was planned to demolished at Trinity Plaza, it led to great concern among the tenants and groups like ours because we were going to lose 360 units of rent controlled housing. In response to that threat, I asked Supervisor Chris Daly to introduce legislation to prevent the demolition citywide. Early in December we were planning to re-circulate a special election for June 2005. The end result was that I got a call from Jack Davis, representing Angelo Sangiacomo, who said we've been fighting so long, what if we save all your rent-controlled housing? Well, keep in mind nowhere in the history of California, I don't believe anywhere in the history of America, has anyone built new housing under rent control. They might have build it under Federal, but not under rent control. Of course, State law forbids rent control in new housing. Angelo was suggesting that he would agree voluntarily with a deed restriction for rent control and that all housing would be replaced on site and none of our tenants in the building would be displaced because the minute the building was ready they would move right over. In fact in a subsequent agreement negotiated by Supervisor Daly, the builders are going to pay for the move and the tenants can take all their furniture to the new place as well. That assurance made a big difference. It looked like we could work out something that would be that rare opportunity for people who have been historic adversaries to come together. After all we've said about him [Mr. Sangiacomo], I'm willing to step forward and make peace. If we did the 15% affordable, we would end up with 275 affordable units in this project. Instead we are getting 350 rent controlled units. When you say you could work out a better deal, how come no better deal has ever come? Who could afford to build rent controlled?  Where would they get financing? The truth is if you do not have the wealth of Angelo Sangiacomo, this project wouldn't happen. There is no public money in this. Trinity is giving up 200 commercial parking spaces it already has.  Remember when you take away parking spots from revenue it is already getting, that means that you are taking millions of dollars out of the project.

name_raw: Harvey Hacker, Architect for the Project Sponsor
comment: I want to thank whoever arranged this little memorial to Sue Bierman. I appreciate it. This project has an interesting story socially. The sponsor is an OB/GYN nurse. She worked in San Francisco long enough so that the present audience might include people who were delivered by her as babies. She lives in a house on Cesar Chaves and bought the project as an investment in the 1980's. She is approaches retirement. She is experiencing mobility problems due to a knee injury, which is affecting her ability to work. Her mobility problems are exacerbated by the steep grade of the block. She has decided to provide for her retirement housing by moving to the flat block of Duncan Street, which includes the subject project. We designed a unit for someone with impaired mobility with elevators and a modify kitchen and bathrooms if needed in the future., The project includes the second unit, which will be the essential key that permits and ordinary working person to afford to build such a house. James Gabbard I live on 27th Street, which is behind the property in question. What appears to me is that the design of the new building is commiserate to the building to the east. That building is out of proportion to the other buildings in the neighborhood. Most are the size of the building to the west of the subject property. I really think to keep the neighborhood flavor as it is, we need a building the size of the one to the west. Silvia I live on Duncan Street and am raising my daughter as a single mother. I oppose the current plan and the staff report's failure to look at the character of Duncan Street. There is a failure of due process. The report doesn't mention that these are earthquake Victorians. The buildings are where the railroad went through. Most are modest with a living space setback from the sidewalk. Most have vegetation in the front. This two-unit building is larger than any single living space or any unit or home on the block It is probably bigger than the combined living space than the two units. None of this is addressed in the staff report. The staff report failed to address community concerns. A number of people made calls and emailed. None of this was described in the staff report. Paul Ordi I encourage you to approve the project. It's not out of scale with the neighborhood and would be a benefit to the owner and the neighborhood. Barbara, property owner I've been a nurse for 30 years and it's hard to believe I will need assistance for myself. I am trying to live as independently as possible. The house is ADA accessible. I am working any angle I can to live independently and hope you approve it. Mary I think you should approve her project so this lovely, beautiful lady can be a productive part of San Francisco, which she loves an adores. Pamela Robins I am speaking in favor of the project.

title: Rev
comment: We are proud to have the opportunity to talk about a project that we feel strongly meets the needs of so many people in San Francisco. Affordable housing is critical as we read and look at television in this City and we want to provide, good effective efficient affordable housing. We have already built a 52-unit housing complex that has received some nine national awards. It's already built. We've had it for six years. I remember someone saying, within six months this place will be torn down. I invite anybody, I don't care where he or she is from, to come and see our present housing complex. It's one of the best in urban America. There is no doubt about it. I am proud of it and what we did and how we did it. What we are doing here with the two units seems a direction we must go. It's a direction that says, people come first and make sure there is enough room and space and there are bathrooms and special kitchen facilities. It's a direction that says that the poor might benefit from it. And not only the poor, but the homeless; we are talking about families. We are talking about two units that will meet a great need in the City and County of San Francisco. I'm proud to have the opportunity to come to you. I want you to know that when you pass this and give us an open door; you are really doing something for a large number of people. We have been to the Board of Supervisors and community groups and all sorts of responsible community groups in the City because we wanted them to know about our project. We wanted them to know about the housing complex and we've been there. I think you will find we have gone to people from every walk of life and especially to people who will benefit from this project. Let me say that we are concerned about the people who are still outside. The people who had to stand on concrete and the people who sleep on the streets and the people who have nowhere to go. In the future we need a housing complex where people not only have shelter but we also have places for people to go and be proud of what they are doing, reading rooms, places for them to eat. We've got some of these already but places for them to be a part of what we call the community. This is our community. We want to continue to make it our community. We must include those who are in great need. Paula Collins, Development Manager for the Corporation In response to a question from Commissioner Lee on why didn't we build higher? Commissioner, we thought it made sense to look at the existing zoning in this area. And the fastest way to get the housing was to stay within the building envelope dictated for this site. That doesn't mean we will not continue to build housing. We will be back. [Name not given] I live at 55 Mason Street where this spot is going to be. Any housing in San Francisco is important. Some of the people come here from different states and countries. What we see now is you got the homeless. The SRO's are catching a lot. We want to make sure it includes bigger units. The CW building - what I learned in the last five years is that they have the best houses. They get their own kitchen and more functions. We also want you to pay hand to SRO's they are celebrating 5 years. We are in the City and going through a lot of changes now. Unstable managers and people moving. Space is important. You get out of these small spaces. We join San Diego, L.A. and San Francisco. We have SRO's in New York. We are joining the world market of Asia and Tokyo; of people who live in smaller spaces; building new buildings. Space is important.

Rod Henmi for Michael Willis Architects

I would like to begin by first putting the building into context with this first drawing.

You can see this is the project site that the neighboring buildings actually open to the sides, rather than backyards.

 They don't face backyards.

These two buildings have their back windows face the side.

As you can see, the buildings on our side of the street are of varied heights.

There is some consistency on both sides of the streets for a street wall approximately 80 feet high. On the other side of this street, there are varied heights.

These buildings are 80 to 90 feet high and they are directly across the street from our site.

This building is oriented 90 degrees to the sight plan; the same way as the site plan orientation.

We tried to orient our building in a manner that was sympathetic and comfortable for the neighboring residents.

This building is an L shape with the largest base facing the south to grab the most available sun.

 That's the major courtyard.

 The other is used as a space and quiet reading space.

The idea is that the building would be reinforcing of the street wall by this height that's compatible with the two sides.

There is a deep recess in the middle that creates more texture to the street.

It has a recess that leads to the opening at the base and projecting bay window that has a slight taper to lead to the entry space.

Paula Collins

As his delegate speaker in this particular project, as with the prior project we have fantastic development partners.

We would be remiss in not mentioning TNBC who is the development partner on the first building and this one is Millennium Partners.

We have the ability and opportunity to take advantage of great collaboration with the community, an organization that's respected with an excellent development partner in the City in Millennium.

 And two architectural teams that can meet and work jointly and do address many of the issues that Commissioner Moore has raised about having design that reflects the quality of the support of services and the living environment that will happen in the building and the neighborhoods.

We are joint venturing this project.

We, being Glide Economic Corporation are not only venturing with them to not only satisfy but to take advantage of their enthusiasm for creating affordable housing, really creating the affordable housing.

They became aware of the Reverend and his activities and a partnership was formed.

They are contributing equity to make this project happen.

We believe because of that contribution we can deliver units faster than what was communicated.

School Principal It's my privilege to look to the future in the City addressing the needs of the parents in the community. Due to the fact that both parents have to work we want to offer services to the families in the area with preschool. We are looking to use one our buildings that currently is used as a construction supply and workshop and is being rented out by one of the people in the Perish. We are looking to use that facility to convert to a preschool. We sent out surveys to all of the families in the neighborhood asking for input. We had neighborhood meetings. We followed up with the survey and got a tremendous round of support from the neighbors that had been surveyed. It's my hope we can move forward with the project. We have postponed this three times to resolve a dispute with a neighbor which we resolved. We will continue to work with the neighbors. We want to address the needs of the entire community and serve them in an educational sense. No name I am the neighbor at 1358 14 th Avenue. I am very opposed to this. Not with preschools in general but a preschool next door to me. The parking right now on our block is terrible. I have my driveway impacted every day. All neighbors I talked to are opposed to this. Rick Riley I have a construction company in San Francisco and use that facility with agreement from Saint Anne's for vehicle storage. I am not in opposition to a daycare. It's great for Saint Anne's. I am concerned about the parking.

DR requestor I live at 2636 Bush Street. We have lived there for 20 something years. We have major issues with the plans submitted and we brought it to the applicants' attention in August. They never bothered to change the plans and submit the plans, even though our objections were made known to them, until our lawyer sent them a letter. Then they changed the plans. I need assurance that they will do& I want to make sure I don't have a bad experience after the fact. I would insist that they give me a new roof after they are done. As far as the rear deck, we don't object to that. We object to the stairs. The way they propose it it's sticking out like a sore thumb in the middle of an open yard. We prefer the stairs on the east side where there is a solid fence. A friend of the family His wife sent me here saying he is not a good speaker. The roof problem & I have been hearing this story for seven months. The stairway - in the original drawing it was on the left hand side of the house, looking from the back. If the stairway stays on the left side they eliminate noise and privacy problems. The architect should be able to solve the problem simply.

Owner We feel this is a simple addition to the home. There is no way for us to access the backyard from the main living area. We spend most our time in the room.  It's at the back of the house. We feel we have been forward and open with our neighbors and trying to address their concerns. We are hopeful that you approve the project.

Policy Director of the Planning and Research Commission (SPUR) I really support the plan of action that has been laid out by staff. I think it is sensible. I enjoyed hearing your discussion about the organization by topic so you see the plan an an integrated whole. I appreciate the suggestion there should be a time certain. I know there are a lot of people who want to attend the hearings and it is a helpful way to move forward. SPUR has been supportive of the Better Neighborhood's planning process. The reason we are supportive is because it provides certainty to the community. It provides certainty to project sponsors and they know what to build. I believe the process is laid before you and it will allow us the time to participate in the discussion. I hope you move the initiation forward.

President of the Duboce Triangle Neighborhood Association We are 20% of the plan area. We are cited as a model neighborhood in a transit rich environment. We support long range planning. We support a plan sensitive to the needs of our neighborhood. I want to acknowledge the work the Planning Department has done.  They have been accessible to us. We have spent a hundred hours on this plan. We have some concerns remaining.  Some are serious. The historical survey. We feel we are inches apart. We are looking at a 30-year plan. I don't understand why three more months will kill this thing. When you rezone you give a benefit to the property owner. If it comes back different you will take away the benefits from the property owner and there will be a reason for the property owner being in a historic district. We feel zoning is good for preservation. We want to do a full court press and understand where the properties are that are historic and where the individual sites are. When do the infrastructure improvements kick in? We welcome the way the process is going in terms of set dates. Separate parking and historic preservation. There will be workshops with the neighborhood groups to vet out the issues. We support that if there is a real chance to make changes.

Served on the Task Force of the [Duboce] Triangle Area. We have been working with staff for about a year. Our initial comments cane in August.  We have read the plan and all the material. We have offered thoughtful suggestions on how this plan should be amended so that can we can embrace it. Right now we are not ready to embrace this plan. We are here to appeal to you, the Commissioner, as you go through this, to listen to our rational. To hear why we think in our neighborhood certain aspects of this plan will be detrimental rather than beneficial. We researched and read it an thoughtfully considered the issues. We had heated discussions in our group on whether the plan is good for us or not. We need these amendments and I hope over the next few months that the staff and the Commisison will be open to the changes we are putting forth, which we think will improve the plan and protect our neighborhood. As you review this information, please keep in mind that there are rebuilding and reweaving neighborhoods that are putting things back together. The Triangle is not that the type of neighborhood.  It's already a pretty darned good neighborhood and it doesn't need a lot of reweaving or improvements. Certain things can be detrimental. One to pick on is the huge increase in density that's proposed for our residential neighborhoods. We are a neighborhood of two and three unit buildings and two and three stories.  This would change the density to what the property owners decide within the [new] bulk and height. To get the six units is pretty easy within those parameters. That's a doubling of the density in our residential neighborhood. That's a point we have a concern about. We look forward to working with you, bringing our points to you and hope you and the staff will be open to the amendments so we can embrace this plan. Peter Cohen I think the schedule of hearings is reasonable if everyone is ready to do a lot of work. I want to make sure that when folks talk about the length of time this has taken there was a significant dead zone for a couple of years while the EIR was being prepared. I don't want there to be a mistake that people feel they need more time. We are starting into a new phase of dialogue. The hearing schedule is reasonable. We are looking at an adoption packet. This is not flipping the pages.  It is reading new materials.  It's the adoption-codified stuff.  It's an experimental plan. Rincon was 12 development projects. This is a neighborhood.  We are prefabricating fragile virtues in the case report. We have to be careful about the fine-tuning process and list to the community who lives there. I think they should be taken seriously. This is about getting it just right. A few quick issues: Mid-block open space - a lot of the development impact in residential neighborhoods happens in the interior of the block.  You don't see it in the street but you feel it when you live there.

Better Neighborhoods Plus provided the structure for the public benefits program. How do you deal with the up zoning included in the plan?
On the Board of Haze Valley Neighborhood Association I'm not speaking for them. Dennis Richards mentioned this was a 30-year plan. I hope it doesn't turn into a 30-year planning process.

I've been involved since 2000 since it started. The Planning Department should be commended for their outreach and the number of community meetings they have done. I'm in support of the plan. I think we need to really move forward as expeditiously as we can. I live a half block off Octavia Boulevard. There are a dozen parcels waiting to be developed. My neighborhood is in limbo.  We are waiting for the plan to go forward before things can be completed on Octavia as well as other sites. We need to consider the plan and the information we have before us. The schedule proposed by the planning staff allows us to do that. I hope we will not delay this plan any further. Tes Wellborn, Haight-Ashbury Council I have participated in the Market/Octavia plan for the past six years and have seen several hundred people participate in that plan. As you move forward, take into account all those people who have been at meeting after meeting. This plan benefits all of San Francisco. We support the plan. But the plan is translated into zoning and community improvement planning. I urge you to have additional meetings besides the public hearings where the details can be worked out. We need to put things in that are not there now that modify some things and move fast at the same time. Hopefully in a couple of months we could have this tied up. Let's get some of these things like affordable housing and the community benefit's plan nailed down more tightly and better. Sue Hestor Looking at your scheduled, hearing number 2 is a killer hearing. One of the unfortunate thing this Commission does is call up the entire calendar. Items 1-6 the only time the public has time to comment is a one three-minutes opportunity on areas on Market Street. There are huge differences in the communities on Market Street and huge difference in the topic items. If you are going to do things right commit yourself that each item is called separately, show you don't' really cheat the public. I think you need to have serious discussions on the backside impact on Imrket Street. You need to see the scale of what is there.  That includes photos. You don't have that now unless you got different things than I did. You really need to see what is the impact where you have large buildings on Market Street and small possibly historic buildings to the rear. Those are the issues I have dealt with over my cases. There needs to be appropriate attention paid to the non-Haze Valley part of this. I don't think it is unusual to say you maybe should have a little bit of explanation on issues particular to neighborhoods that are not the core. Marilyn Amini I feel it is good you will mail to every resident that will be impacted. I'm wondering, will the mailed notice be neighborhood specific? That touches on the question as to how you are going to organize discussions. As Sue mentioned, there is a huge difference in communities and how they are impacted. If you will communicate in your notice area specifically and how those particular areas will be impacted, people will feel they are given adequate notice. Gary Weiss, President, Upper Market Association, EDPA, the CDB and Merchants of Market and Castro. I want to speak as a small business owner in the Castro. I wish I could have participated earlier on. None of the groups I am affiliated with were aware. The main point is parking. We don't feel the point of view of Eureka Valley residents were included.  We need more parking not less. The small businesses in the area are suffering from lack of parking spaces. When large projects are in the works regular information forums are a tool to educating the public. This one, despite the neighbors in the eastern end of the plan, is lacking. We are asking for a delay. This will ensure a large element of the plan area will have the ability to review the plan and input its views.

comment:
We don't have a formal presentation, but want to thank you for working with us over the past weeks.

 We have eliminated all of the parking as requested and retained a LEED-Platinum rating.
We oppose any reduction and/or shadowing of downtown open space.
Please reconsider your decision to grant a 46 percent height bonus as a reward for a LEED certified building.

name_raw: Bill Sauro, President, Barbary Coast Neighborhood Association
comment:
Go green and get spot rezoning.

 That is a terrible precedent you will establish with this project.
Our neighborhood association has strong opposition to any increase in height along the waterfront and we do support a full EIR.

I'm here to support the staff's original recommendation from November 30, 2008 to disapprove the rezoning of this site because the height increase is in conflict with the current zoning; the proposed design is inappropriate with surrounding buildings; and the new building will cast new shadows on open space.

It is a dangerous precedent to allow any development along the Embarcadero to have an exemption to the height limit.

 Developers will be happy to develop their projects as green to get that bonus.

 We'll end up with Miami Beach down there.

I live in the area and I'm here to support the project.

 The building is a jewel box and will enhance the Embarcadero.
We are so worried about you approving this because of the spot zoning.
Follow the Department's original recommendation and disapprove the rezoning of this single site to accommodate this project.

I am in strong opposition of the rezoning of 110 The Embarcadero from 84 feet to 130 feet.

 Spot zoning sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the very purpose of the city's Waterfront and General Plans.

 Please require a full EIR

I'm here to speak against the spot rezoning.

 The Waterfront Plan might be an old document, but it can be reviewed with broad public input and updated if need be.

 That has not been done.

name_raw: Dave Osgood, Rincon Center Tenants Association
comment:
We oppose this high rise.

 It is out of place in this special and important area in this city.

 It is out of scale with the Audiffred building.

resident of Rincon Towers The current vacant building is an eyesore and something needs to be done and it's nice that a developer is doing something with the space and its wonderful that the parking has been removed.

 Why does the building have to be so large and why are we going against the city guidelines and policy?
I urge you not to reclassify 110 The Embarcadero for new bulk and height.
We are unique and we should not let developers go against our General Plan

I oppose this exception to the General Plan and the Waterfront Plan.

 It's a bad idea to grant this spot zoning.

SF Tomorrow Offered to take the commission on a tour of the waterfront.

Do not pit the environment against the neighborhood.

 That is what you would be doing with this project.

 If you give people a density bonus for LEED buildings, you're going to have a fight between greening the city and over building the city.
This is a project of spot zoning and spot zoning is generally not a good idea.
We ask that you reconsider your decision and require that a full EIR be done for this project.

An 84 foot tall building with mechanicals is tall enough.

 I urge you to disapprove this reclassification.

 This would be a terrible precedent and why?

 What decisions have they made to make this building so expensive?

The rational for the height is the building.

 That is a rational for spot zoning.

 It should be what is the context for the heights in the Downtown Plan?

representing the Project Sponsor As far as shadow and wind impacts being significant, based on shadow and wind studies in the Mitigated Neg. Dec, they are found not to be significant.

 As far as inadequate public review, there was public notice of the availability of the Preliminary Mitigated Negative Declaration and of the underlying studies and anyone who had an interest could review them.

 This is not spot zoning.

 This is a single site rezoning.

 We already have a LEED-Platinum certification and it's in the materials sent to you.

 We do comply with the Downtown Plan policies.
